Messages.Author: Tom Duncan
Messages.Body:
Assamite Clan Newsletter
January, 2006
By Tom Duncan

I hope the New Year finds you all healthy, wealthy, and wise.

I'll start off this month's offering with a look at some of the
fringe (that is, not specifically Assamite or Quietus, but perhaps
relevant) cards for Assamites from Legacies of Blood. Following that
you will find Part 2 of my essay, "Managing Assamite Combat," and a
decklist that hopefully demonstrates some of the points I've
discussed.

Legacies of Blood Honorable Mentions:

Kamiri wa Itherero
Clan: Akunanse (group 4)
Capacity: 10
Disciplines: ABO ANI FOR OBF pot qui
Laibon: Younger vampires must burn 1 blood to attempt to block Kamiri.
If an ally blocks Kamiri and combat occurs, burn the ally at the end of
the action.

Here's another option for that OBF/QUI/ANI crypt, though a pricey
one. Kamiri's FOR also makes him(?) an option for inclusion in a
crypt with Antara, Joe Hill, or Janni. His special combines nicely with
Dawn and Day Operation, which will make blocking very unpleasant for
vampires and a 'last hurrah' for Allies.

Ubende
Clan: Ishtarri (group 4)
Capacity: 7
Disciplines: CEL PRE for obf qui
Laibon magaji.

Ubende joins Jack Dawson and Joaquin Murietta in the non-Assamite
obf/cel/qui club. His PRE and [for] make him an excellent
co-conspirator for Joe Hill, Antara, Janni, and Vardar. He can also
assist Olugbenga in Laibon politics with his title. A quality vampire
at a fair price, I'd pick him over any given 7-cap group 1 Prince.

Aversion
Type: Reaction
Requires: Valeren/Celerity
Cost: 1 blood
[cel] Reduce a bleed against you by 1.
[val] Burn X pool to reduce a bleed against you by 2X+1.
[VAL] Only usable when a minion is bleeding you for 1 or more. Put this
card on the acting minion. You still control this card. This minion
gets -1 bleed when bleeding you. Any minion may burn this card as a +1
stealth (D) action.

This is a very nice card for the !Salubri, and the outferior provides a
large percentage of Assamites with access to bleed reduction. While
not nearly as efficient as having AUS, it might be more useful than
grafting AUS on with skill cards when using group 3 and 4 Assamites
(only Antara has it, and at inferior). Confusion of the Eye [obf] is
free, and, despite its capacity limitation, is probably the better card
for most Assamites in Group 3-4. Still, having a universally applicable
bleed reducer available to the majority of the clan is an improvement
over Banner of Neutrality, balanced nicely with a cost of 1 blood, thus
assuring that neither of them see much play in our decks. Thankfully,
there are no Assamites with [val], so I won't have to re-visit high
school algebra to try to figure out the inferior application of this
card.

Death of the Drum
Combat
1 blood
Only usable at long range.
[cel] strike: 1R damage
[mel] Strike: 2R damage, only preventable by cards that require
Fortitude or Visceratika.
[MEL] As [mel] above, and the damage is aggravated.

While this card gives Daughters of Cacophony a much-needed combat
boost, I don't think it does anything for the Assamites that
Projectile doesn't do better. With access to Quietus and Taste of
Death, this card just isn't for us. Note that the [MEL] application
of this card is actually better than Taste of Death. I may have to
declare shenanigans...*

Healing Touch
Type: Action
Requires: Obeah/Celerity
Cost: 1 blood
+1 stealth action.
[cel] Untap a younger vampire you control.
[obe] Add up to 2 life to an ally, not to exceed his or her starting
amount.
[OBE] Rescue a vampire from torpor, and that vampire gains 1 blood from
the blood bank.

Reminiscent of Precognizant Mobility, and probably just as useful. I
would like to find a way to use this card to improve the usefulness of
Fida'i, but I can't.

Leapfrog
Type: Combat
Requires: Spiritus/Obfuscate
[obf] Maneuver, only usable to go to long range.
[spi] Maneuver.
[SPI] Strike: combat ends.

Assamites commonly fight their battles at long range, and if that is
your plan, here is the card for you! Since Selective Silence and Behind
You! are both only good for the first round of combat, Leapfrog can be
useful with the "new look" Assamites ("Look, mom, no
Celerity!") if you intend to try press combat. Combine with a Trap to
help ensure you get to round two and beyond.

Squirrel Balance
Type: Action Modifier
Requires: Spiritus/Celerity
Cost: 1 blood
[cel] Only usable when the action is announced. If blocked, range in
the first round of the resulting combat is automatically set to long.
[spi] Minions without flight or Spiritus get -1 intercept when
attempting to block this action.
[SPI] As [spi] above, but those minions get -2 intercept.

Squirrel Balance will be very useful in long-range combat builds, or
builds that just want to avoid being Grappled and punched for 18. It
costs blood up front, but the utility of your potential blocker knowing
range will be long could be advantageous if it causes more "no
block" responses than your actions would otherwise warrant. An
excellent card choice for a deck designed with Pool-damaging D actions
and streamlined combat. Keep an eye out for Janni, with a mouthful of
acorns and a Sniper Rifle, running along your telephone wire...

Vulture's Buffet
Action
Requires: Spiritus/Obfuscate
+1 stealth hunt action. If this hunt is successful, the acting vampire
untaps.
[obf] Remove a minion or retainer in any Methuselah's ash heap from the
game to move 1 blood to this vampire from the blood bank.
[spi] As [obf] above, but move 2 blood.
[SPI] As [spi] above, and you gain 1 pool.

The untap clause here is nice, but the qualifier could be troublesome.
Provided you intend to burn at least one minion or retainer early in a
game, including a Vulture's Buffet in your library could be
beneficial. If you are running multiple copies of a unique ally or
retainer, you can definitely plan to use the Buffet for some
multi-action support, confident that those extra copies of your unique
Ally will end up in the ash heap. An excellent card choice for
self-destructive allies and retainers like Ghoul Escort, Zombie, and
Escaped Mental Patient. It's a hunt action, so you can use Succulent
Vitae, too! A nice rare. Don't read the spi/SPI part - it'll only
depress you.

And now, the long-awaited sequel:
Managing Assamite Combat, Part 2

Defense: It wins championships.

It is a commonly heard sports cliché that the best defense is a good
offense. This is not necessarily true in the early stages of a V:TES
game, where your predator and prey are not the same opponent. Putting
extra pressure (in terms of minion removal) on your first prey will not
affect your predator's ability to pressure you. It is important to be
patient, as I discussed last month. Since it might be a few turns
before you push left, you'll have to survive in the meantime.
Consider the following:

1.Your predator is not your target. It is important to defend yourself
against your predator's devious schemes, but always remember that you
need him there. If you destroy his ability to defend against HIS
predator, you will soon face his newly-fortified ouster. It is highly
likely that you will have to run at least one of his minions through
the cheese grater at some point, probably early on (depending on how
many minions he has in play and what they are trying to do to you).
Many players will rush their predator first almost as a rule. I prefer
to see what his intentions are first, unless his vampires have
Dominate, in which case they simply must go.

Your deck should be built to bloat at least a little, and unless you
are fighting to stay in the game, you should concentrate more on posing
a threat to your predator than actually crushing his will. After you
block and atomize one of his vampires, or rush and liquefy one of his
pesky bleed-bouncers, be sure to point out to him the various threats
he faces from HIS predator. You want to keep him at a minion
disadvantage with regard to his predator, but with enough ready minions
to be able to survive. This is where the contract mechanic can shine.
Many decks focus on the abilities of one vampire, and if you can lock
that vampire down with a contract, you put your predator on the ropes
and get him playing defensively. If he steps out of line, that
permanent rush is available for the judicious distribution of what
for.*

Don't feel like you have to block everything your predator does, or
avoid taking pool damage at all costs. Unless he's trying to oust
you, your predator is merely your last prey, and one more victory point
for you. Remember - your actions have the most profound effect on the
game in that they remove minions from the ready region. Managing your
predator properly can be the difference between winning the game and
handing it to another player. You want to SURVIVE your predator, not
OUST your predator.

2. If you can be bought, be sure to advertise your price. You might be
the only combat deck at the table. This likelihood increases
significantly if you are playing in a tournament. Surrounded by
streamlined ousting machines, there may be a player at the table whose
deck is trumped, and whose presence at the table only serves to build
steam for his predator. It might be in your best interest to prevent
this from happening. It will depend upon your assessment of your
ability to deal with the strong deck, to sacrifice an action or two to
do something about it, and your strength relative to your predator and
prey. If you think you can trash a vampire controlled by the dominant
methuselah, be sure you get your money's worth. The player you are
helping might be able to give you a beneficial referendum, allow you
access to his KRCG, offer to rescue your prey's Famed vampire for you
- who knows. You might also get a juicy counter-offer, too.

Some players simply don't make deals. In this case, you do what you
have to do to get your best advantage. You want maximum VPs, but if in
giving one up you don't compromise your ability to oust your prey,
that's okay, too. You don't HAVE to set the table up for a cascade
oust and a table sweep. Often with combat decks, you will be better
served by letting the big bleeders or anti-combat builds leave the
table. If you think you can cause a stalemate with surgical cross-table
minion removal, AND it works to your advantage, consider it.

4. You need to be able to block. Especially true in tournaments, the
ability to stop your predator's key actions is, well... key. In a
casual game, you may have the fortune of sitting next to a player who
is experimenting with a trick bloat build, and is content to just
survive until heads-up play while accumulating minions. You will do
better to not count on this, and instead plan to block some actions,
likely with some stealth on them. Since your combat build has little
room for transient intercept, you will need some permanent sources.
Market Square is our clan specialty, and any of the media locations and
the staple Sport Bike will aid in this endeavor. Whether it come from
master cards or equipment, permanent intercept will afford you the
opportunity to block actions at crucial junctures, notably political
actions and vital non-directed actions taken by your predator or prey,
such as rescues and mandatory hunts. If your opponent is packing
stealth modifiers, you are likely NOT going to catch him anyway, and
might be doing him a favor with a block attempt by allowing him to
cycle stealth. If you played patiently early on, you will know this
already, and can concentrate on removing the offending vampire from the
ready region instead.

4. Don't be the bad guy. While sportsmanship is important to any
friendly game, it's not what I am talking about here. You want to
avoid being perceived as a threat to the whole table. If you jump on
your prey as soon as he has three minions but fail to oust him, or beat
your predator silly on consecutive turns, every player will be looking
at you as a threat to their game. When you block your predator, you
don't have to cycle every available combat card you have. Consider
the game balance, and your position in it - that is, your ability to
survive your predator's strategy while defeating your prey's. While
obliterating minions Tasmanian Devil-style is fun and has its own level
of rewards, you might find yourself with a hand full of the wrong cards
afterward. Often, leaving your predator's vampires low on blood or
forced to hunt is sufficient. Save the good stuff for your prey.

5. You have to be able to untap. Taking minion actions is even more
important with a combat build, as the majority of your cards will only
move on your turn. You probably won't be rushing with every action
until you are ready to oust, but you will likely have hunting or
gearing up to do until you reach that point. Reaction cards will
hopefully flow into your hand while you finish equipping or fighting,
but the high number of combat cards in the deck means reactions are few
and farther between. When your hand dictates it, you might have to
leave a vampire untapped simply because you can't risk combat, and
hope that the threat of being able to block is enough to prevent you
from having to. Most of the time, if things are going well, you will
want to take as many minion actions as you can every turn. It is
important to be able to untap, either during your minion phase or with
reaction cards. Black Sunrise offers Assamites (any vampire with
Quietus, actually) an excellent means by which to untap when an action
is announced. Even if you know you can't block it due to inherent
stealth, your vampire will be left untapped after the block attempt
fails, ready to block those free directed actions your predator thought
he was going to be able to take, or to play reaction cards on
subsequent actions. Untapping a vampire outside of the untap phase is
key to maximizing their effectiveness. Not paying proper attention to
this aspect of your build could have you watching the end of the game
from the sidelines.

Bring it on
You have three or four Assamites in play. You've managed to get some
permanents on the table, and have a pretty good idea what your
opponents are playing. You've convinced your predator of the folly of
incurring your wrath, and your prey has had to push pool back to his
minions with his Blood Dolls instead of using them to bloat, thanks to
you. Time to make your move? Consider the following:

1. Do the math. What is it going to take to knock your prey out of the
game? Can you do it this turn? If you have Tension in the Ranks and a
Fame in play (for example), how much pool damage can you do? One trip
to torpor for the famous vampire would cost your prey five pool by the
time his untap phase comes around. If you can rescue and dunk the same
vampire for a second trip to torpor, you increase the damage to nine
pool. Add Dragonbound, and you can do ten pool damage with three minion
actions. Are there any weenies you can torporize for pool damage? Is he
likely to be able to block? While lunging in this manner is preferred,
it will probably take you two or more turns of concentrated effort to
get your oust, even if your prey has fewer than ten pool. Remember -
he knows it's coming. During this time, your grandprey will likely
enjoy a reprieve from any pressure that your prey was putting on him.
As he is your next prey, it is important to keep the pressure up until
you get the oust. Khabar: Glory can be very useful here, because if
your prey is ousted on his turn due to Tension in the Ranks or
Dragonbound, you will get your bonus Pool.

2. You will have to survive your predator's response. When you go
all-out on your prey, your predator will respond, especially if you
don't get the oust. Be prepared to suffer some pool damage,
regardless. If you get lucky enough to cycle into some reaction cards,
all the better. When you make your move, though, your hand should be
set up for combat. If you are within striking distance of being ousted
yourself, you must decide if it's better to take the plunge, or try
to improve your position. However, giving your prey time to draw into a
Giant's Blood or Minion Tap (or both) could just as easily end your
game.

3. Stay focused. If you absolutely ruin your prey by putting all of his
minions in torpor but don't oust him, you give the rest of the table
a chance to decide your fate. They can agree to burn the famous vampire
and hinder your ability to do pool damage to your prey. They can agree
to steal your locations, sink you with referendums, or choose you as
the target of all bounced bleeds. If your prey has enough pool to
survive a round of your bleed actions, or can pull pool off of
uncontrolled vampires, etc, you might end up sitting at a side table
telling the event host how close you came to getting a VP. You don't
get extra VPs for burning or knocking all of his vampires into torpor,
either. If possible, use one of his vampires as a punching bag and try
to maintain the appearance that the poor sod still has a fighting
chance in the grand scheme of things right up until you can oust him.
This is where a little stealth can go a long way. When you are moving
in for that re-dunk on world-renowned spelunker* Isabel DeLeon, getting
past the desperation blocker could make all the difference. Swallowed
by the Night is one of the most versatile Obfuscate cards for clan
Assamite for this very reason. I also find Cloak the Gathering to be
useful in crypts where not every vampire has Obfuscate.

Ok, now what?
After you get your first prey ousted, you can go to work on your next
prey in much the same manner. Hopefully, you still have about half of
your library and you survived the table response to your push with your
minions mostly intact and your pool somewhere around ten. The
difference now is that you can be less patient. That's not to say you
should throw caution to the wind, but at this point in the game
vampires are generally low on blood, and players will be working to get
their own VP before they are ousted themselves. You should be wary of
your grandpredator getting an oust, as this will give him some
momentum. While you would ideally like to systematically eliminate each
methuselah's star vampire and then proceed to mop them up in sequence
for the sweep, most of the time you will have to look at trying to get
one more oust if you can, and then surviving the heads-up duel. Your
advantage will be that as resources dwindle and keeping vampires in
play becomes more and more important, your ability to survive, and even
thrive, in combat will ultimately give you more freedom to act and
block.

Of course, stories of your deck's combat prowess and how it ruins any
chance anyone else has of getting anything accomplished will have
traveled throughout the room, and your situation in round two will be
that much more difficult. A majority of players, in my experience,
would much rather be ousted with minions in play. Getting burned on an
action or referendum is less humiliating than just sitting there,
unable to play any cards, while some jerk is repeatedly taking
advantage of your lack of combat cards. The player who transfers out of
a game is indeed more frustrated than the player who bemoans his lack
of a Wake With Evening's Freshness as the reason for being ousted.
Players would rather play than sit and watch their game end. If you
make it to the finals, be prepared to experience a significant level of
that wonderfully intangible "table hate."

As you can see, playing a dedicated combat deck is far trickier than it
might seem. I have found that it truly tests a player's overall V:TES
skills, and can be the most rewarding style to play when you are able
to do it well. It will not always go well for you, that I promise.
Arika WILL Kiss of Ra you, Brujah WILL punch you for 8, aggravated
damage WILL send your star Assamite to torpor, and stealth bleed WILL
oust you by turn seven. It is important to remember that you have
chosen what is still the most difficult path to victory, and to
maintain the right attitude toward it. Once you develop the proper
patience to allow you to assess a table, find the right balance between
offense and defense, and learn to recognize when to make your push for
the VPs, all you really need at that point, come to think of it, is
Kali's Fang and a bunch of Blurs.

Messages.Author: quickbeam
Messages.Body:
Excellent Newsletter. I had been eagerly awaiting the second half of
your essay on combat.

> Managing your
> predator properly can be the difference between winning the game and
> handing it to another player. You want to SURVIVE your predator, not
> OUST your predator.

This seems to be the place where combat players earn their bad
reputation most often. A stealth bleed predator slips by with a bleed
for 4, and the rush player freaks out and starts to move upstream like
spawning salmon. It is definitely important to have a bloat element in
most combat decks, especially if you lack bounce, because as Tom points
out eventually you have to take it in the teeth.

The other element besides bloat that I like in combat decks to 'manage'
my predator is S:CE. Often, you have been representing your combat
prowess, and your predator has to build up to a decent combat hand.
When they finally have the stones to come at you, it is especially
gratifying to disable a prerange card (carrion crows) and an evil
strike with a combat ends. This saves your real combat for your prey.
Preternatural Evasion isn't as strong as Earth Meld, but it is still a
great card.

> Save the good stuff for your prey.

> 2. You will have to survive your predator's response. When you go
> all-out on your prey, your predator will respond, especially if you
> don't get the oust. Be prepared to suffer some pool damage,
> regardless.

This is important. You are going to take losses, and that is why you
need some bloat abilities. One of the nice things about a combat deck
is that you often have the ability to recover and rebuild, even when
things go wrong.

> Ok, now what?
> After you get your first prey ousted, ...

> most of the time you will have to look at trying to get
> one more oust if you can, and then surviving the heads-up duel. Your
> advantage will be that as resources dwindle and keeping vampires in
> play becomes more and more important, your ability to survive, and even
> thrive, in combat will ultimately give you more freedom to act and
> block.

This is the true advantage of a combat deck, the ability to move about
more freely during the ugly endgame.

> A majority of players, in my experience,
> would much rather be ousted with minions in play. Getting burned on an
> action or referendum is less humiliating than just sitting there,
> unable to play any cards, while some jerk is repeatedly taking
> advantage of your lack of combat cards. The player who transfers out of
> a game is indeed more frustrated than the player who bemoans his lack
> of a Wake With Evening's Freshness as the reason for being ousted.
> Players would rather play than sit and watch their game end. If you
> make it to the finals, be prepared to experience a significant level of
> that wonderfully intangible "table hate."
>

Risking potential argument and flame wars, why do you all think this
is? How is getting minions smoked so much different than getting bled
for 8? Crying about a lack of Wwef is blaming a loss on the rain,
instead of on yourself. Likewise, not being ready for combat is a flaw
in deck design.

Admittedly, it would be frustrating to see a player total all your
minions, and then set up your grandpredator to oust him, you, and the
rest of the table, but combat doesn't need to be played that way. Even
if it is, I fail to see the difference between that situation and a
stealth bleed predator who stalls after 1 oust. Lately I've been
thinking that maybe all of this stems from an overemphasis on
collecting victory points and an underemphasis on winning the game (I
don't mean sweeping per se).

This article, and the one that preceded it, can definitely help people
play combat responsibly. It is slightly more challenging than just
adding 3 change of targets to a bleed deck, but more gratifying as
well. Thanks a ton for the newsletter. I'll keep an eye out for the
next one.

-Dave Clooney

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1136490518.5...@g44g2000cwa.googlegroups.com>,

quickbeam <dcqui...@yahoo.com> writes:
>Risking potential argument and flame wars, why do you all think this
>is? How is getting minions smoked so much different than getting bled
>for 8? Crying about a lack of Wwef is blaming a loss on the rain,
>instead of on yourself. Likewise, not being ready for combat is a flaw
>in deck design.

At a very simple level: players like to play.

Let's assume that we've both spent 15 pool on minions and have 15 left.

Scenario A: you have a weenie Night Moves Obfuscate deck. You're
pecking away at me solidly. However, your actions don't stop me acting.
You come and bleed me and I'm down to 12 pool, but my my Count Ormonde
can still play a Temptation (for example).

Scenario B: lock-down. You're playing a deck specifically designed to
thwart my ability to take actions but NOT a significant combat deck.
For example, Banishment, Reality, Sensory Deprivation, Pentex Subversion
etc. From your point of view, this could be a very solid deck and a
strong candidate for a win (which is why you've played it, I guess).
But if you get a lock-down action or master through, it stops me playing
my game. Now Count Ormonde can't play Temptation, and even though
you're less tangibly close to an oust, I'm more frustrated because I
can't do my thing.

There are a few similar strategies of denial - card denial, blood
denial, library exhaustion and relatively hefty combat - which can annoy
players for similar reasons. It's not that they're necessarily more
powerful than a solid bleed deck, it's just that they stop me playing my
game if I don't have enough of a deck to defend against whatever it is
you're doing to me.

--
James Coupe

> How is getting minions smoked so much different than getting bled
> for 8? Crying about a lack of Wwef is blaming a loss on the rain,
> instead of on yourself. Likewise, not being ready for combat is a flaw
> in deck design.

Let's not oversimplify all this shit. No deck can be "ready" for
everything. Trying to be ready for everything will only leave a player
ready for nothing. You pick your poison: which forms of combat will you
try to be ready for? And "none of them" is frequently a reasonably
successful option, IMO, depending upon the local metagame.

Anyway, to get to the answer to your question, it's just this: if
you attack me with a combat deck I'm not ready to handle, I'm screwed.
I'm screwed whether you succeed or fail in ousting me. If you take
all my minions off the table but get ousted before me, I still have
no chance. If you merely torporize most of my minions before you get
ousted, I have no chance. If you merely torporize SOME of my minons
before you get ousted, I probably have no chance. Just by the fact
that my predator or prey is a combat deck that I'm not totally ready
to defend against, I'm at least somewhat screwed and quite possibly
totally crippled whether you succeed or fail. That makes you bad
news to have as neighbor.

On the other hand, decks that attack pool directly frequently (not
always, I'll concede, but frequently) will leave its victim in viable
operating condition up to the moment he's history. Typically,
unless I got heavily bled right from the start (counting
political KRCs/ConAg/etc as "bleeding"), I would have a working
complement of minions when I was ousted. Of course, if I get
ousted without ousting anyone else, it doesn't make a shred of
difference. But against this kind of predator, I may well get
some VPs before I die. And if my predator comes close but
fails (for instance, gets close to being ousted himself and must
leave all his minions untapped on defense), I may well go on
to sweep the table. Neither of these scenarios is likely to
happen against the same predator doing combat.

To me, the difference is manifest and abundant. I don't know
why people don't seem to understand this better, but I often
find myself reminding people that in a multiplayer game,
interactions between player pairs are not necessarily zero-sum.
In fact, often they aren't. What's bad for me in our last combat
ain't necessarily good for you. Or, more precisely, it's often
not AS good for you as it was bad for me. And it may well be a
disaster for us both.

Fred

Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> To me, the difference is manifest and abundant. I don't know
> why people don't seem to understand this better,

'Cause I still don't think it is as different as you think it is.

If you compare midgames, then yeah, losing 18 pool worth of vampires to
torpor is different than losing 18 pool (and usually, in the mid game,
losing 18 pool of minions leaves you crippled but still in the game and
still with some sort of options--not necessarily good ones, but they
exist; losing 18 pool generally ousts you, leaving you with no options
at all).

Early in the game, however, the difference is very minimal.

You get out a 4 pool minion and I dunk him, you are out 4 pool (and 4
transfers--not insignificant, but a trade off for having a minion in
torpor which is a greater asset than no minion in torpor). On the other
hand, I bleed you for 4, you don't get out that 4 pool minion. If I'm
an angry rush deck and I torp your first 12 pool of minions, you are at
18 pool with a bunch of minions in torpor. If I'm a turbo bleed deck
and I bleed you for 12 instead, you are at 18 pool with no minions in
torpor (I'd rather have the invested minions, mind you--someone might
save them...) or you are at 6 pool with 12 pool of minions. That might
be a defensible position, sure, but in either case, you have lost 12
pool.

Sure, people like having minions, and with minions, you might be able
to defend yourself from the mad bleed predator that has bled you for 20
in the first 4 turns, where having 20 pool of minions torped is likely
to result in you dying quickly, or being totally hosed even if you
don't die. But in either case, you are probably dead anyway--a weenie
DOM bleed deck is going to ruin your game just as much as a vicious
Rush deck. The main difference is that the weenie DOM deck kills you
fast, and then you get to go eat a sandwich or play a pick up game; the
vicious Rush deck makes you sit at the table useless longer.

-Peter

> On top of THAT, is the fact that the first vampires tranferred

Is this really always true? If so, then why? If you always speed out
your key vampire first, and this turns out to be to your disadvantage,
it's your fault for playing poorly, not mine for rushing and/or
diablerizing him when you have no defenders.

Generally speaking, the "key" vampires tend to be rather on the large
side, too. I almost always get out a one or two turn vampire (or even
2 such minions if pressed) before influencing the 3 turn vampire so
that I have some minions who can defend my pool, bleed early, fight
other weenie minions on possibly preferential ground, and exhaust my
opponent's combat cards to clear the way for the more valuable minions.
I don't think I'm alone in doing this either. If you (in the generic
sense, of course) don't do this, maybe you need to adjust your thinking
about the opening.

In Chess, beginners have a tendency to develop their Queen very early
in the game. This seems logical at first, because it your most
powerful piece and you want to use it as much as possible. However,
any competent player will tell you that this is folly (except in some
bizarre openings typically played only by extraordinarily cocky
experts), and that the best approach to the opening is to stake a
position in (or attacking) the center with your pawns, then develop
your minor pieces, and then bring out the Queen (often times castling
before doing so). Of course, Chess and Jyhad are very different games,
but some of the same principles may apply. Swap "pawn" for "weenie"
and "minor piece" for "midcap" and it's pretty clear what I'm saying...

involved choosing two vampires that I was intending to play with for
the whole game, leaving two others as backup or if I succeed at bloating
through ousts or other means later on in the game. If a combat deck
just takes out the first two totally, then I have to use some of my backup
pool that was intended as my buffer against ousting in order to get

choice will not be as good as either of the first two. So here is
yet another way losing straight pool to bleeding is not as bad as
losing vampires. And it doesn't matter which of my first two vampires

it doesn't matter whether it gets demolished first or second.

I hear this argument a lot. I think it's ridiculous. When playing game X,
other tables don't exist. If you allow other tables to exist, then you're
allowing something outside of the game state to affect your play. Strictly
speaking, you shouldn't do this. Ability to play another game should *not*
affect your opinion of the validity of playing combat or any other
strategy which progressively stops your game. That it does is your
failing, not that of the "slow deck" player.

Many people who play combat decks do so because it is fun and challenging
to do so. These decks and players are still playing to win. And, unlike
your lame bleedzooka/votezooka(tm) deck, they're trying to actually try an
under-represented and low-power mechanic. Have a bit of respect for these
folks. . . Without them, this game would more closely resemble others that
we'd rather it not. Moreover, combat provides a much-needed check and
balance on more direct strategies. It's a necessary leg of the triangle,
even if it is underpowered.

> out of 100 come back and actually win; play carelessly and try to get
> ousted as soon as possible (sometimes harder than it seems); or pack my

> bled.

The latter two aren't actually aligned with any notion of playing to win.
If you're closed-minded enough to suggest that you can't come back from
such a table state, perhaps you ought to hone your ability to consider
table balance. Often, a path to victory is not merely 1/100 when crushed
by a combat deck. Challenge yourself to win under duress and two things
will happen: 1) you will learn to play better; and 2) you will win more.

> Neither are really "fun". If you're out in 20 minutes, then what, you
> find another table (or, chances are, the game won't be lasting that long
> if it turned 4-player in 20 minutes).

Huh?!? This _exactly_ the reason to go all (WTF does "gangly-eyed" mean?!?)
whatever and froth at the mouth. This is precisely the same thing as getting
ones minions torped and being left without a key resource that will fuck
them over whether their predator succeeds or fails. The fact that their
library will wind up being too small to last long enough to sweep the
table is the same thing as losing one's minions.

OK, it may be _slightly_ different in that you might, for instance,
maintain enough library to still make your first oust. If your
library-eating predator goes away fast enough, it might not even hurt

You find it amusing when both types of decks cause more or less the
same problem? It makes perfect sense to me. It's the same non-zero-
sum issue. If you (as the combat deck or milling deck, whichever) succeed
and oust me, fine. But some of the time, however good your deck and
however well you play it, you will fail. And when you fail, your
neighbors are still much more likely to be screwed in some way than
if you were just a bleed deck that failed. Thus, people hate to be
the neighbors of these types of decks with very good reason.

Fred

argue that whenever you are at the point where future VPs are extremely
unlikely, you can freely choose the method in which you obtain them.

The real problem with these options is that they aren't really nice things
to do. It's remarkably unfun to stare at a pile of pool counters and
slowly eat them up, knowing that there was a player sitting there once.

Of course, in tournament play the choice is always #1, because if all else
fails, you can hope for the 1/2 VP. Unless it was absolutely clear, my
comments refer to casual play.

> If you're closed-minded enough to suggest that you can't come back from
> such a table state, perhaps you ought to hone your ability to consider
> table balance. Often, a path to victory is not merely 1/100 when crushed
> by a combat deck. Challenge yourself to win under duress and two things

I don't really feel that the content or tone of this paragraph was
utterly appropriate.

>> Neither are really "fun". If you're out in 20 minutes, then what, you

>> long if it turned 4-player in 20 minutes).
>
> I suppose your notion of fun doesn't involve thinking. On second
> thought, it's probably best to ignore all that I've said. . .

Well, neither was this, for that matter.

> since you'd have to think about it.

No, you're perfectly able to play your game until the exact moment when
you're decked. It's much like stealth-bleed in this case. A bleeding deck
has done nothing to you until you've lost your last pool, in a certain
sense. In a much more *real* sense, you have suffered from absolutely
*nothing* until you're decked. And that's when you die.

Until then, you can play your game. You have minions, pool, and cards in
hand and deck.

> OK, it may be _slightly_ different in that you might, for instance,
> maintain enough library to still make your first oust. If your
> library-eating predator goes away fast enough, it might not even hurt
> you at all. And because it hurts you more the longer he stays in the
> game, this is exactly the reason to go straight backwards when you get
> such a predator and not stop 'til he's history (or you are).

Milling decks generally give their prey about 12 turns of deck. If you
can't generate an oust in this time, well, you were probably screwed
anyway. If he's ousted within that time, yes, you are hurt. But, you're no
more hurt than a strong bleeding predator who's left you at 3 or 5 pool
before being ousted herself. I fail to see the difference.

>> Anyway, I find it generally amusing that the same people who often
>> argue and whine about combat decks then turn around and whine about
>> milling decks, though they provide a categorically different play
>> experience in either case.
>
> You find it amusing when both types of decks cause more or less the same
> problem? It makes perfect sense to me. It's the same non-zero- sum
> issue. If you (as the combat deck or milling deck, whichever) succeed
> and oust me, fine. But some of the time, however good your deck and
> however well you play it, you will fail. And when you fail, your
> neighbors are still much more likely to be screwed in some way than if
> you were just a bleed deck that failed. Thus, people hate to be the
> neighbors of these types of decks with very good reason.

milling, and one which "prevents you from doing so", i.e. combat decks)
are lambasted equally as being something that is irritating to one's
playstyle. For most such people, they should realize that they want to
play only when their predator is unable to harm them. . . In other words,
they want a free win.

I don't see how failure to oust with *any* strategy leaves their prey in a
better position than any other. A bleed deck that fails leaves its prey
low on pool. Similarly with a vote deck. Combat decks leave their prey
poor of minions. Milling decks leave you poor of library cards. Again, how
is any of these other notions of being screwed any worse than another?

Most people I know froth at the mouth at a bleedzooka predator. Know why?
Cause they don't get to play their game then either.

>

I don't want to just "play my game until the exact moment I've been decked."
Who told you that was what anybody cared about? Somebody else, I guess,
not me. The point was, with a bleed deck, I still have chance to win
until the moment I'm ousted. I could be down to a single pool and still
oust other people and get back into the game. Or bloat because most decks -

> It's much like stealth-bleed in this case. A bleeding deck
> has done nothing to you until you've lost your last pool, in a certain

What? You're telling me I'm in the same condition if I'm down to a
single pool as if I'm down my last 10 library cards? If you can't
see the difference between the two situations, it's no wonder you
can't figure out anyone else's point of view about this. You can
come back from being down to your last pool. If you're down to
your last 10 cards during a relatively early part of the game, you're
almost certainly a dead Methuselah walking.

> Milling decks generally give their prey about 12 turns of deck. If you
> can't generate an oust in this time, well, you were probably screwed
> anyway.

First of all, that's just wrong. I've played any number of games where
I've existed longer than that without ousting anyone and eventually
won. Secondly, even if I wangle a single oust, it's unlikely I'll get
another one if my library's exhausted.

Seriously, I don't see what problem you're having seeing this. Are
the implications of the library exhaustion a mill deck causes really
so hard to grasp? I'm confused why I'm even getting an argument about
this. If a mill deck works at all well, then it screws its prey whether
it wins or loses. Why is that so hard to understand?

> I find it amusing that two decks (one which lets you play your game, i.e.
> milling, and one which "prevents you from doing so", i.e. combat decks)
> are lambasted equally as being something that is irritating to one's
> playstyle. For most such people, they should realize that they want to
> play only when their predator is unable to harm them. . . In other words,
> they want a free win.

I'm not sure what "such people" you mean. But I think you're getting
confused about the fact that the combat deck which is at least successful
in its tactics, takes its victims' ability to function away immediately.
The mill deck takes it way later on, very suddenly. But it takes it away
just as inevitably. It doesn't matter that my deck still functions at
this very moment. I know that I need library to function in long run.
If I don't have it, I'm just as screwed as I am with combat deck.

The bleed deck may put you on the brink but you can come back from it.
There are almost no ways to recover library and none that can solve
what the mill deck does to you.

> I don't see how failure to oust with *any* strategy leaves their prey in a
> better position than any other.

Well, sorry. Clearly, there is a difference. As I said earlier in the
thread, many people understand the difference intuitively even if they
don't understand how it works exactly. I think you're intellectualizing
it away and just plain ignoring the obvious point.

> Most people I know froth at the mouth at a bleedzooka predator. Know why?
> Cause they don't get to play their game then either.

I suppose the argument could be made that a super-bleed deck doesn't give
its prey enough time to set up a defense and play their game. If the
that bleed deck has no defense and winds up getting ousted before it
ousts, then I'll give you that the same kind of irritation is in order
for more or less the same reason. That's just screwing your prey to the
benefit of your predator. (I know because I'm guilty of this with some
of my lousier decks, frankly.) Most good bleed decks that people play
aren't like this. And if you get bled out lightning quick because your
predator has a good deck and wins quickly, that's not the same thing.

Fred

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:


Take a look at your original assertion. You wanted to be sure that you
could still "play your game", which is something that a combat deck seems
to deny you. A milling deck does not prevent you from playing your deck.

As a separate point, you can still oust other people and get back into the
game with 10 library cards. Largely because many many many games end up in
a player getting an oust before 12 turns are up. Pulling a second vp with
a restricted library is no different than any number of other instances of
attrition. In this case, a reduced library size is offset by the fact that
you tend to have little to no pool/minion pressure. You can make full use
of 30 pool whereas others must be careful of it.

There is still hope to win even if you have been milled to about 10 cards.
Presumably you knew that this would happen and you changed your strategy
accordingly over the course of 12 turns. You may have emphasized
permanents, taken opportunities to remove key minions while you were
fairly certain to still have cards, made deals in anticipation of being
decked, blocked or removed or slowed your deck's milling. . . . (There are
quite a number of available and versatile responses to milling decks. I
mention a few later on.)

>> It's much like stealth-bleed in this case. A bleeding deck has done
>> nothing to you until you've lost your last pool, in a certain sense. In
>> a much more *real* sense, you have suffered from absolutely *nothing*
>> until you're decked. And that's when you die.
>
> What? You're telling me I'm in the same condition if I'm down to a
> single pool as if I'm down my last 10 library cards? If you can't see
> the difference between the two situations, it's no wonder you can't
> figure out anyone else's point of view about this. You can come back
> from being down to your last pool. If you're down to your last 10 cards
> during a relatively early part of the game, you're almost certainly a
> dead Methuselah walking.

Don't try to slip in "relatively early". It just doesn't happen with
milling decks. You're going to lose your deck (generously speaking) by
about turn 12. That's not early. That's mid for a few games. That's
mid/late for most games. That's late for some. That's not early for most
games that fit in a 2 hour time limit, if any.

Of course you're not in the *same* situation. But, at the same time,
you're not in a hopeless one. You're in a situation that's uniquely
different from being at 1 pool but presents similarly interesting options.
Your resources are constrained (one way or another) and it's your job to
pull something through with that. Are you telling me that never ever ever
ever in your life would you ever feel as if having more pool at the cost
of some extra cards in your ash heap isn't a good tradeoff?

Finally, for the record, you're almost certainly a dead Methuselah walking
with 1 pool too. (Some cards are even designed to exploit your newfound
weakness; see also From a Sinking Ship.)

>> Milling decks generally give their prey about 12 turns of deck. If you
>> can't generate an oust in this time, well, you were probably screwed
>> anyway.
>
> First of all, that's just wrong. I've played any number of games where
> I've existed longer than that without ousting anyone and eventually won.
> Secondly, even if I wangle a single oust, it's unlikely I'll get another
> one if my library's exhausted.

Sure. Lots of people have. How likely is it that you'll earn a vp on just
1 pool? How likely are you to win a table with 1 pool? Is that more or
less than playing with fewer cards? Have you factored in the fact that you
can go whole-hog forward because your predator chose not to do pool
damage?

For the games in your career that you have won, can you give an average of
how many cards were in your deck at the time of winning? Those cards,
whatever they were, were completely useless. Wouldn't you have loved to
have extra pool instead of those dead cards? Your milling predator gives
you that advantage off the top. He has to mill more than that number
before he ever affects you. You get free pool for his silliness.

> Seriously, I don't see what problem you're having seeing this. Are the
> implications of the library exhaustion a mill deck causes really so hard
> to grasp? I'm confused why I'm even getting an argument about this.
> If a mill deck works at all well, then it screws its prey whether it
> wins or loses. Why is that so hard to understand?

If a bleed deck works well at all, it screws its prey whether it wins or
loses. If a vote deck works well at all, it screws its prey whether it

wins or loses. Why is that so hard to understand?

My point is: library exhaustion is *no more* of a resource winnowing
strategy than any of the other three (bleed, vote, combat). You are
afforded certain luxuries with a miller behind you, namely little other
tangible pressure. Even if you ignore the pressure angle to an extent,
you're still watching a predator invest card slots and time to fielding an
orthogonal strategy which doesn't impact the normal operation of your deck
until it's basically too late.

> I'm not sure what "such people" you mean. But I think you're getting
> confused about the fact that the combat deck which is at least
> successful in its tactics, takes its victims' ability to function away
> immediately. The mill deck takes it way later on, very suddenly. But it
> takes it away just as inevitably. It doesn't matter that my deck still
> functions at this very moment. I know that I need library to function
> in long run. If I don't have it, I'm just as screwed as I am with combat
> deck.

I'm not confused about anything: a combat deck constrains you throughout
the game by reigning in minion actions. A bleed/vote deck constrains you
throughout the game by reigning in options, which are concretely
represented by pool counters. A milling deck constrains you *once you're
decked*, and not a moment before. If ANY strategy were to get close to its
goal and fail, it would be devastating to you. It should be, because they
were close to their goal.

The fact that your deck functions *NOW* is huge! You get to play. You get
to earn vps. You get to move for a win. And, if you can get out from
underneath the power structure in 10 or so turns, the mill deck may not be
able to stop you from moving around the table. Remember, it has a predator
too. . . .

> The bleed deck may put you on the brink but you can come back from it.
> There are almost no ways to recover library and none that can solve what
> the mill deck does to you.

There isn't a need to recover library! Get an oust or three while the
thing sets up! Most milling strategies also have standard responses that
one can use to deal with them. Location destruction, blocking, vote
denial, suddens, etc. Many of these are standard defensive mechanisms that
might find their way into a normal deck anyway. You're not up a creek
without a paddle. You can slow or arrest the depletion of your library in
a proactive manner rather than conjuring a scenario where you're dealing
with a fully-teched up predator. And, since milling provides no benefit to
your predator until you're well and thoroughly decked, the resultant
situation can shift the balance of the table in all kinds of ways.

>> I don't see how failure to oust with *any* strategy leaves their prey
>> in a better position than any other.
>
> Well, sorry. Clearly, there is a difference. As I said earlier in the
> thread, many people understand the difference intuitively even if they
> don't understand how it works exactly. I think you're intellectualizing
> it away and just plain ignoring the obvious point.

Sorry, I'm not letting you get away with "clearly there is a difference".
Yes, by the nature of the fact Y isn't X, it's different. But its
consequences in the context of this conversation are *not* different.
Everyone understands that Y is not X; that's what you're talking about.
Those who think about it realize that Y->Z just as much as X->Z; that's
what I'm talking about. I'm not intellectualizing away an obvious point;
I'm telling you that game play allows a great deal of freedom to the prey
of a milling deck. And, that it ain't so bad.

Heck, I would rather be the prey of a milling deck than any other kind of
deck. Bring it on. I would love it. I put Liquidation in some of my decks,
and now I don't have to!

>> Most people I know froth at the mouth at a bleedzooka predator. Know
>> why? Cause they don't get to play their game then either.
>
> I suppose the argument could be made that a super-bleed deck doesn't
> give its prey enough time to set up a defense and play their game. If
> the that bleed deck has no defense and winds up getting ousted before it
> ousts, then I'll give you that the same kind of irritation is in order
> for more or less the same reason. That's just screwing your prey to the
> benefit of your predator. (I know because I'm guilty of this with some
> of my lousier decks, frankly.) Most good bleed decks that people play
> aren't like this. And if you get bled out lightning quick because your
> predator has a good deck and wins quickly, that's not the same thing.

I think you just proved my point. A deck that wins is not part of your
irritation. By definition, if the milling deck wins, you can't fault it
for what it did to you. It had to to win and you were steamrolled in the
process.

We're talking about decks that put a good effort into ousting you and then
fail, either due to poor design, play, or just table state. For these
scenarios, again where decks are unable to oust but make crippling moves
towards doing so, a milling deck hoses its prey in no worse a fashion than
a bleed deck or a vote deck. I'd argue similarly for a combat case, but
I'm willing to concede that for the sake of focusing on milling.

A bleed/vote deck that leaves you at one pool hasn't left you whole and
happy; most likely, you'll be ousted. When you've got 10 cards left in
your deck but a pile of pool and minions to act with, you're likely
ousted. But, you have no less of a chance to win than in the 1 pool case.



Messages.Author: Tom Duncan
Messages.Body:
Weenie *anything* is worse than mid-cap or Star & Support *anything*.
That's a completely different topic.

While I appreciate the lengthy back and forth following something I
authored, I'm curious as to peoples' opinions toward the opinions I
present in the NL, as they apply to this topic. It was my intention to
preach on "responsible combat" (much like 'responsible bleed'), which
focusses on actually ousting your prey while preserving table balance
and even encouraging stalemates between your rivals.
Whirling Dervish or Tazmanian Devil style play can lead to ugly games.
It is my belief that most players of combat deck over-estimate their
predator, and turn far too right far too early. I also think this is
primarily propogated by poor deckbuilding, which leads to an all-rush
game. When you have to do all of your defense during your minion phase,
you are going to make a bunch of enemies, and when it ultimately
doesn't work, you lose, and leave your neighbor broke, sticky, and
confused. I tried to preach on that a little, too.[Diversifying your
combat build, that is]
Remeber the first half of the essay is in the December newsletter - I
could post just the essay in it's entirety if anybody requests it (or
feel free to copy and paste it together and post it yourself). I think
reading the two parts together presents my philosophy on playing combat
fairly clearly, and addresses a lot of issues that have been points of
contention here.
Note that I throw in some thoughts that, in retrospect, I probably
shouldn't have, given that no one can see my tongue-in-cheek. For
example, I say that won't rush my predators' vampires right away,
unless they have Dominate, in which case they simply must go. Granted,
Dom presents it's own set of complications, but I honestly like to keep
even a Dom bleed predator in the game. Any vampire with Superior has to
be nuetered, of course, unless your grandpredator isn't bleeding much,
which makes the Deflections a non-issue (or near-non).

I've seen the "no-minions" response from the prey of a combat deck
before, and it was quite effective. This was a pre-con sabbat War/Cam
Ed tourney, so take that into consideration. But it's why I suggest
paying attention to the Bleed action, too.

> takes an already hard to play concept and socially engineers it out.

There are two ways to look at this. One: rules-wise. I'm at a losing
position, I may choose to lose the way I wish to. Two, assuming the
player wishes to have fun: there is considerably less fun associated
with "playing" a lost game with the likelihood that you're dead anyway
than playing it with actually having some options left.

I'm sure everyone feels the gaping difference between actively
participating in the tug-of-war that is VtES and having no power left,
being empowered or cast aside at the sole discretion of the other
players. The level of control (and active strategising) is
significantly different.

> The original point you made implies a form of social engineering which
> in turn takes the fun out of the game for *someone else*.

Well, I'm getting curious what the implication I made was. ;)

> So long as they're playing to win in a given game, socially engineering
> out decktypes is a poor strategy. I don't know why you can't have fun in
> a situation when you're well and truly hosed. For me, this is when I
> really get down to it and start churning out possibilities. The greatest
> elation for me comes in winning from a losing position. Do you prefer to
> give up when the odds seem stacked against you?

Depends. Mostly I just want to play my deck because I feel like doing so.
I assemble it because I want to try a given combination of cards and
strategies. Most of the time I prefer tables where I can play my game
regardless of whether I win or lose.

I guess winning a card game is not the absolute goal for some of us?

though, you know, because all this time, for some stupid reason, I
actually
thought you were in fact talking about the topic of this thread. Silly

> grandpredator? Hunt? Wall up? Wait for your prey to tap out? The options are
> often limited, unless you thought to add some during the deck-building
> phase.

There are plenty of options. Here are a few:

Bleed for 1 a lot.

Refuse to play any stealth and inform your grandprey that she should leave
a minion or two untapped to block your bounced bleeds. I do this a lot.
My grandprey starts untapping and I announce I'm planning to do some big
bleeding on my turn, but won't add stealth. Almost any deck can arrange
for the most basic defenses given the notice "expect a 0 stealth bleed of
4 heading your way on my next turn."

Yeah, hunt a lot and bloat with Blood Dolls, bring out more minions and
bleed for 1 a lot.

Get blocked, tap out prey (Faceless Night on a bleed for 1), then go for
the big bleed.

Any good player will assess the situation and adjust her strategy
accordingly. Sure, sometimes heaps of bleed bounce will result in one's
grandprey getting ousted, but there are certainly measures one can take to
mitigate things. A good deck will include other tools (Spying Mission,
Anarch Troublemaker, etc.) to avoid ousting its grandprey, but even
without those there are options other than putting on blinders and
bleeding for 6 at stealth every turn.

Matt Morgan

"Matthew T. Morgan" <far...@io.com> wrote

>
> There are plenty of options. Here are a few:
>
> Bleed for 1 a lot.

I rarely see that from S&B decks. The temptation to lay down the bleed mods
is too strong for most people, I guess.

> Refuse to play any stealth and inform your grandprey that she should leave
> a minion or two untapped to block your bounced bleeds. I do this a lot.
> My grandprey starts untapping and I announce I'm planning to do some big
> bleeding on my turn, but won't add stealth. Almost any deck can arrange
> for the most basic defenses given the notice "expect a 0 stealth bleed of
> 4 heading your way on my next turn."

Reasonable. I don't usually see that kind of consideration from most S&B
grandpredators. Usually they're content to bleed irresponsibly without a
care in the world, in my experience.

> Yeah, hunt a lot and bloat with Blood Dolls, bring out more minions and
> bleed for 1 a lot.

That would assume including Blood Dolls in the first place and having them
installed on the vampires in play.

The situation I am talking about is long after the deck construction phase
and when we have little control over what cards are in our hand. Assuming a
Malk S&B, let's say we have no Blood Dolls in-play or in-hand, a hand full
of DOM and OBF and nothing else. I suppose you could hunt anyway, or make
someone an anarch cardlessly perhaps, but that's not really going to do much
(usually) to help them achieve their greater goal of winning that game.

> Get blocked, tap out prey (Faceless Night on a bleed for 1), then go for
> the big bleed.

That assumes the S&B deck has a Faceless Night or has a prey who actually
bothers blocking unstealthed bleeds for 1. Conventional wisdom is not to
bother blocking (unless playing an equivalently intercepty deck). And if
they're not blocking unstealthed bleeds for 1, the S&B deck is back to
square one. Their deck is still effectively stalled.

> Any good player will assess the situation and adjust her strategy
> accordingly. Sure, sometimes heaps of bleed bounce will result in one's
> grandprey getting ousted, but there are certainly measures one can take to
> mitigate things. A good deck will include other tools (Spying Mission,
> Anarch Troublemaker, etc.) to avoid ousting its grandprey, but even
> without those there are options other than putting on blinders and
> bleeding for 6 at stealth every turn.

I agree, of course. The problem is that it is very easy to look at a given
table state and say "That deck could use Spying Missions" but at that point
in time it is a moot statement. The player either hasn't included them (and
shame on them) or does not have them readily available (which can't really
be helped). I don't know if that is enough of an excuse for bleeding
irresponsibly, mind you, but there may not be as many options available as
you imply above.

S&B decks bleed heavily at stealth exactly because that *is* what they are
designed to do, so the player in David's example does have a point.

(Though I am all for such people designing more interesting decks.)

Cheers,
WES

Messages.Author: CthuluKitty
Messages.Body:
> While I appreciate the lengthy back and forth following something I
> authored, I'm curious as to peoples' opinions toward the opinions I
> present in the NL, as they apply to this topic. It was my intention to
> preach on "responsible combat" (much like 'responsible bleed'), which
> focusses on actually ousting your prey while preserving table balance
> and even encouraging stalemates between your rivals.

Since few people have directly responded to the main point of the
newsletter, I'll go ahead and say that I really liked it. The points
about patience and responsibility dovetail really well. It strikes me
that one of the biggest misconceptions about playing Jyhad is that the
best way to play your deck is to cycle through cards as fast as
possible. This might often be true for bleed and vote decks, but it is
wildly far from the mark for combat based strategies (including but not
limited to rush). If you can get away with it, bleeding your prey for
6 at 3 stealth is almost always a good idea. Likewise KRCing and Voter
Capping for 8. Clobbering another player's vampire might not always be
such a good idea, and you really have to be a much more shrewd and
observant player to win with a strategy that does that. Regarding the
latter, it seems that a lot of players simply stop paying attention
from when their prey's turn ends and their predator's turn begins, and
then reevaluate what's going on at the start of their own turn. This
is problematic in that it wastes time, which as a "slow deck" player
really irks me since it reduces my chances of winning in a tournament
game. It also leads to (or is suggested by) a style of play that
ignores table dynamics for a focus on ousting uber alles.

The very fact that there's been so much complaining about irresponsible
combat in this thread is evidence that your point needs to be
considered. It may very well be that the players making these
complaints have primarily witnessed bad, or irresponsible combat
players. When it gets right down to it, the problem isn't combat; it's
bad play. A bleed or vote deck in the hands of a bad or irresponsible
player is equally dangerous (or moreso), as many people are willing to
attest. It may very well be that combat lends itself to bad play more
than other deck types because it so hard to manage correctly.

I'm also willing to venture the guess that the people complaining about
combat decks are probably accustomed to low combat metagames, where
combat decks tend to be seen as a nuissance--and often are. These
players might do well to play or observe a few games in the high combat
environment (the online version is a good way to do this for those who
can't travel). The types of things you see happening in combat in such
metagames are very different. My general impression is that combat
decks in low combat metagames tend to be focused very heavily on
offense with little defensive at all, relying on the assumption that
their enemies will be easy targets--mono potence rush decks are a great
example of this. Decks like this get totally obliterated in high
combat metagames, because people are prepared to defend against their
attacks and fight back with a vengeance. The decks that do well in
high combat games tend to rely on highly flexible combat packages, with
a lot of defense. Cards that work as offense and/or defense are great
for doing this--examples include Drawing Out the Beast, Theft of Vitae,
Stutter Step, Side Strike, Indomitability, Blood of Acid, Typhonic
Beast, etc. When you play combat in this environment, you're much less
likely to go head long rushing at people. Combat is more of a tactical
assett and less of a strategy. When it gets right down to it, it
really strikes me that high combat vs. low combat metagames are almost
like totally different games that happen to share the same rules.

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> People intuitively know that having a combat deck as a neighbor screws them worse than
> decks that attack their pool directly.

But they are intuitively wrong. If they have no combat defense, then
having a combat deck as a neighbor screws them worse than a deck that
directly attacks their pool. If they do, then such decks don't screw
them more.

Losing 20 pool by turn 6 is going to kill you far quicker than losing
20 pool of minions by turn 6. Yeah, losing 20 pool and having a few
minions in play as the prey of a bleed deck might leave you in a
defensible position, but if you have no bleed defense, you aren't in a
defensible position (which is likely why you lost the 20 pool in the
first place). You are just losing. As you will be ousted very soon.
Conversely, if your predator has a brutal Rush deck, and you can defend
yourself, then you don't lose 20 pool of minions, and are in a
defensible position.

The issue comes from what you can turn into a defensible position. If
you can stop a heavy bleed deck, then you can make a defensible
position out of 5 pool and some minions, but if you can't defend, you
get wiped out. If you can defend yourself from a Rush deck, you aren't
going to lose so many minions, and you'll have a defensible position to
work from. If you have no dfense against the offense in question, it
doesn't matter what causes you to lose the 30 pool--you still die
either way.

-Peter

I love the "no-minions" response. I mean, not that I use it, or that I
love if it's used against me, I just love the idea of it - it's
hilarious. ;) And it can really shut down a poorly-built rush deck,
especially one that relies on a big vamp or two, rather than midcaps or
weenie-rush.

At this point in the game, though, I think every combat clan has at
least some decent access to ousting mechanisms, such that a well-built
deck shouldn't need to be *all* combat. (I'm not disagreeing with your
point, just adding my two cents.)

Blood Brothers are one of the biggest "combat-monster" clans, and they
have Walk of Caine. Brujah have presence bleeds or votes, Euro-Brujah
have dominate instead. Anyone with Animalism can at least go with Army
of Rats and Tier of Souls. Assamites may have had a hard time up until
KMW, but now they have a number of different paths to ousting - Alamut
turns your bleeds for 1 into voting power - so maybe you add a few
KRC's to your deck; Khabar: Glory gives you an extra +1 bleed, and a
nice reward if you oust, Flurry of Action lets you bleed and do
something else, Songs of Distant Vitae gives you inherent stealth and
might give a +1 bleed. Some other stuff in KMW doesn't directly help
you to oust, but can facilitate other paths - Black Sunrise lets you
tap out and still be able to block (better than Wake, in *most*
situations), and Deviki Prasanta helps you get your vamps all tooled up
- especially if you choose to tack on an "ousting" discipline, like
dominate or presence.

Sabbat clans (and Sabbat Assamites, if you choose to focus on them)
have Pentex Loves You!, and every clan has access to stuff like the
bleed retainers, Laptops, Computer Hacking, etc. Robert Carter
deserves special mention for combat clans that use Steal Blood strikes
or Taste of Vitae, as you can put that blood to good use.

I think that the way of the New Combat Deck is to toolbox a little.
Those bleed modifiers will help you oust your prey, and can double as a
pseudo-rush if you want to get blocked. Bloat and defense can allow
you to focus more on your prey, since, as you mention in your essay,
you don't have to accomplish all of your "defense" by rushing your
predator on your turn. Weenie combat decks can still afford to focus
entirely on combat, because their sheer number of minions is their best
offense. But Star Vamp decks and even mid-cap combat decks almost
require some toolboxing, or else they *do* tend toward what you
mentioned - beating up a lot of guys and then dying with no VP's.

Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
pd...@lightlink.com wrote:
>
> Dubious rushing of folks is bad for everyone. Probably it is more
> noticable, due to people A) Not liking to have to play combat defense
> like they have to play bleed defense and B) People not liking having
> their minions get beat up, but bad play is bad play, regardless of what
> type of bad play, and Rush combat is no more responsible for bad play
> than any other deck strategy.
>

Not really. The problem pure rush decks have is that their defense
consists of either:

1) Promising to erase your predator if he becomes a threat to you.
or
2) Actually erasing your predator.

If I'm playing pure rush I'll bring out a minion, look at my predator,
and ask myself 3 questions - Does he have any stealth at all? Can he do
a lot of damage to my pool? Is he a soft target for my combat? If I get
two or more yesses I'll go straight to smashing him. Only once he's
firmly under control do I need to even look at my prey.

In the early game I want my prey going after HIS prey with his fight or
bleed or whatever - until I don't have to watch my back and I'm good
and ready to mop up the table.

Is that irresponsible? Or is it trying to win? The problem Rush decks
have is eliminating their predator is the only defense they've got.
Other defensive options may allow you to protect your pool while
leaving your predator intact.

-Ben Swainbank

people are allowed to start with their minions on the board and
transferred out vs. not on the board and still in their uncontrolled
areas and with less than four minions in their uncontrolled areas.

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
> I didn't refuse to admit that. That isn't Ankur's argument. He's
> trying to suggest that losing most of your library basically isn't any
> kind of disadvantage. I didn't see where he was trying to claim having
> 12 turns of non-harassment was a compensating advantage.

Fred, I've mentioned many many times that you gain an advantage by not
having minion or pool pressure for 12 turns. I'm not sure how you got away
without seeing that. It's clearly written in my recent post, but here are
at least FIVE quotes from a post that you responded to which speaks of
having a compensating advantage. Let's get started:

"As a separate point, you can still oust other people and get back into

the game with 10 library cards. Largely because many many many games end

up in a player getting an oust before 12 turns are up. Pulling a second vp
with a restricted library is no different than any number of other
instances of attrition. In this case, a reduced library size is offset by
the fact that you tend to have little to no pool/minion pressure. You can
make full use of 30 pool whereas others must be careful of it."

(consequence which you claim I didn't mention is black and white)

Here's another:

"You're in a situation that's uniquely different from being at 1 pool but
presents similarly interesting options. Your resources are constrained
(one way or another) and it's your job to pull something through with
that. Are you telling me that never ever ever ever in your life would you
ever feel as if having more pool at the cost of some extra cards in your
ash heap isn't a good tradeoff?"

(tradeoff of pool for cards implies consequence which you've stated I
didn't include)

Here's another:

"Have you factored in the fact that you can go whole-hog forward because
your predator chose not to do pool damage?"

(rhetorical question designed to hint at the point that I must have
forgotten to include)

Oh, here's one that specifically uses the word "advantage":

"For the games in your career that you have won, can you give an average
of how many cards were in your deck at the time of winning? Those cards,
whatever they were, were completely useless. Wouldn't you have loved to
have extra pool instead of those dead cards? Your milling predator gives
you that advantage off the top. He has to mill more than that number
before he ever affects you. You get free pool for his silliness."

(Includes the word "advantage" as a clear consequence of the milling
strategy. In fact, the words are in the same sentence. . . .)

Here's a quote that suggests a non-concrete advantage of having been
milled:

"The fact that your deck functions *NOW* is huge! You get to play. You get
to earn vps. You get to move for a win. And, if you can get out from
underneath the power structure in 10 or so turns, the mill deck may not be
able to stop you from moving around the table. Remember, it has a predator
too. . . ."

(Milling deck may not be able to stop you by its very structure.)

Here's another quote:

"And, since milling provides no benefit to your predator until you're well
and thoroughly decked, the resultant situation can shift the balance of
the table in all kinds of ways."

(This quote is interesting as the *dual* of the argument that you gain an
advantage, namely that your predator FAILS to get one until his schtick
gets going.)
