Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 9 Jan 2006 13:55:20 -0500, Ankur Gupta <agu...@cs.duke.edu> wrote:

>> Sure. Until my last pool is lost, I still have my minions, and can play
>> all of my cards. When I'm ousted, I go to the next table, and continue
>> playing my game, although from a different phase.
>
> See, the point you're not getting is this: the rest of your sentence
> after "when I'm ousted. . ." really shouldn't be part of your judgement
> for the current game.

Okay, allow me to rephrase in a more complicated form.

I am spending t time on a game. (Let's stick to examining a single game
for simplicity.) Also assume that I have x cards total in my deck, y of
those are master or event cards, obviously (x-y) are minion cards. Let's
further assume that my total utility (fun) is directly proportional to
the portion of my deck I can use, the "fun-to-play" parameter of my deck
(let's call it constant "a"), and obviously the time spent playing.

In a "normal" game my total utility is x*a*t. In a game where my minions
are demolished my total utility is y*a*t. Since y<x, my fun is bound to
be less. In fact, since y is usually a fraction of x (say, the ratio is
usually around 1:5), let's say that my total utility is one-fifth.

Even if you do not assume that the choice is between continuing a
low-utility game (perhaps even hoping it will turn high-utility) and
switching to a high-utility game (the way each game starts) there is
still the issue of the threshold utility - meaning, that under a certain
utility level the activity ceases to be appealing. So even if there are
no prospects for making a choice to terminate the current low-utility
game and immediately engage in a high-utility game, but rather the
choice is to terminate the low-utility activity (and assume a generic,
average utility level activity to replace it), the termination of said
low-utility activity can still be desirable.

Even more simply put, I'm sitting down to play cards and have fun. If all
you can do is ruin other people's fun, please don't mind me not wanting
to stick around for that.

Mind you, this says nothing about a well-played combat deck that can
actually win games in even a remotely entertaining fashion. The general
point (which you apparently deliberately failed to get) is quite simply
what I stated some 4 posts ago: If you are playing denial tech, you are
potentially ruining other players' fun. Use it scarcely and wisely,
perhaps even keeping in mind that you make an effort at them enjoying
the game even though you deny them part of their resources.

> Because, if you allow that, you're essentially saying that combat decks
> are less welcome on tables with you on them than otherwise. Social
> engineering hard at work.

Re-reading your earlier posts you lobby heavily beside the "good cause"
- more acceptance for combat decks. I'm not sure that in that light you
have any ground left to accuse anyone of social engineering. Mind you,
I'm not saying that combat decks should not be accepted; try to
comprehend the depth of my stance.

> Besides, I want to argue this issue of "last pool being lost". Do you
> claim that you get to play your game when you're bled for 20? How about
> 15? At which point do you realize that the minions you were able to
> bring out must play defense mode in order to survive?

There is a partial point here, because not having enough pool to set up
does hinder my game.

> Is it considered playing your game?

Yeah, the lines are indeed blurry. I guess the parallel would be between
the relationship of your bloat and the heavy bleed you face, and the
relationship between your combat and the heavy pounding you face. But
all in all, introducing graduality does not really alter the nature of
the problem.

> I never made an "I. Must. Win." requirement. I only postulated that it
> seems that in many cases where you might otherwise feel that you're
> completely dead, you may in fact not be. Playing to win may net you a vp
> even if, during a particular moment in a game all your minions are in
> torpor.

That's a point I'll never dispute. There is always a chance. It may be
slim,
it may be so slim that you can honestly call it "no chance" rules-wise,
but
the shit can hit the fence, and I've seen many heroic comebacks in the
9-some years I've been playing this game. However, I've seen incalculably
more lost positions from which no eventual comeback was made. In fact, the
ratio would probably indeed be around one to a hundred.

>> My average deck has around 15 Master cards and 75 Minion cards. If I'm
>> ousted, I cannot play 90 out of those 90 cards; if my minions are
>> destroyed, I cannot play 75 of those 90 cards.
>
> So, you proved my point?

No; I refuted it.

> Bleeding/voting you out removes the ability to play cards more than with
> combat? Remember, starting a new game isn't a consideration which is
> allowed if one wants to be fair to all players of all decks in *this*
> game.

...but the average utility general activity does present an opportunity
cost. In a VtES club, the average utility general activity is "playing an
average table of VtES". I guess that puts the dot on the I... ;)

--
Bye,

Daneel

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 9 Jan 2006 01:16:19 -0500, Wes <gh...@NYETSPAMmnsi.net> wrote:

> That assumes the S&B deck has a Faceless Night or has a prey who actually
> bothers blocking unstealthed bleeds for 1. Conventional wisdom is not to
> bother blocking (unless playing an equivalently intercepty deck). And if
> they're not blocking unstealthed bleeds for 1, the S&B deck is back to
> square one. Their deck is still effectively stalled.

Depends. If the S&B deck is sending unstealthed bleeds for 1 because the
prey has bounce, the prey can well be stalled on bounce. Bouncing a few
bleeds for 1 might seem to be a good idea to clear the jam, but the bleeds
for 5 that come afterwards might prove to provide some deterrent to this.
Meaning, the S&B deck is bleeding for 1s, and the prey has all bounce
in-hand, unable to play their decks. This is kind of a stalemate situation
that may go either way, but is not, by definition, necessarily worse for
the S&B deck.

> S&B decks bleed heavily at stealth exactly because that *is* what they
> are
> designed to do, so the player in David's example does have a point.
>
> (Though I am all for such people designing more interesting decks.)

S&B can be very interesting. My philosophy when building S&B decks is along
the lines of: all Stealth Bleed decks can bleed at stealth. What
distinguishes one S&B deck from another is the splash options you include.
Usually those cards can win you games. I've done a lot of stuff with my
S&B decks (including resisting or even beating up combat decks,
controlling the table, walling up, etc.).

--
Bye,

Daneel

Ruining fun is determined by sitting down to a game where someone prevents
you from playing by using an accepted 1/3 of the game? That's a bit
narrow, eh? How fun is it for your predator if you whine and complain
while he/she plays his/her deck?

> Mind you, this says nothing about a well-played combat deck that can
> actually win games in even a remotely entertaining fashion. The general

Where entertaining must be defined by you, it seems, and not the
combat-deck player.

> point (which you apparently deliberately failed to get) is quite simply

Messages.Author: Fred Scott
Messages.Body:
"Ankur Gupta" <agu...@cs.duke.edu> wrote in message
news:Pine.GSO.4.62.06...@cipher1.cs.duke.edu...

>>> As a separate point, you can still oust other people and get back into
>>> the game with 10 library cards.
>>
>> No, you can't. You'll run out of library cards and not oust anyone.
>
> I dunno, Fred, with 17 total cards (the hand as well), and the fact that I
> have been able to freely play the cards in my deck for about 12ish turns
> seems like I get to play with about 40-50 cards. That seems *more* than
> reasonable as a means to oust.

(...addressed later...)

...

> I'm arguing that your ability to get an oust is *enhanced*
> by having a predator who doesn't affect your minions or pool for many
> turns. That enhancement is roped in at about the 12 turn mark, but you
> still have a chance to gain vps and win. You are not totally screwed.

Ah, sorry. I quoted you and then totally missed your point. (I didn't
notice it until David restated it. Sorry.)

The compensating "advantage" isn't worth the disadvantage. For one
thing, there isn't much enhancement. In fact, in some ways, it's
even worse. The only library deprivation deck that even comes close
to working is one that concentrates on Slaughterhouses, Harbingers,
and uses their auspex. Since they don't have to go forward for a
long while using this strategy, they're just giving up some master
phase actions to put out Slaughterhouses, and sitting back on both
defense (which will readily include bleed bounces, a form of
offense as well that I'll have to fend off) and stopping everything
I do with intercept. Just doing that alone - without the library
deprivation - is actually another really form of objectionable
neighbor strategy: the intercept wall. Add library deprivation,
and yes, I'm totally screwed. What you're trying to argue is some
form of compensating advantage is at best totally lame and at
worst, more injury heaped on top of injury.

>>> There is still hope to win even if you have been milled to about 10
>>> cards.
>>
>> Not usually, no.
>
> I've won many games with 10 or fewer cards. I've won many games
> with millers as my predator.

I never claimed you couldn't win a game with a miller as your
predator. I claimed that millers frequently screwed their prey
even they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them
as predators. As for winning with 10 or fewer cards, we've all
done that - when we had a whole library of cards to PUT us in that
position. If you mean, you've won lots of games after a miller
hammered your library severly and got it down to 10 cards WAY
prematurely, I can't speak to that because I didn't see the games
you're talking about. There could be lots of reasons - like
your predator's deck sucked and/or he played it badly and/or he
got so unlucky, the milling didn't affect you that much.
Doesn't change anything. For the record, I'm fine with having
a predator who's game is so bad it doesn't affect me hardly
at all. (Though my prey will no doubt hate that.) But if
my predator substantial does what he's trying to do but just
fails to oust me in the end, THAT will undoubtably cripple me
far more than a bleed or vote deck doing the same thing -
which is my point.

>>> Finally, for the record, you're almost certainly a dead Methuselah
>>> walking with 1 pool too.
>>
>> Sorry, nope. Not the same thing. As I pointed out, people can and do
>> come back from 1 pool left all the time. Paul Johnson built a deck that
>> REQUIRES he play with with one or two pool at all times.
>
> I can't assist you with understanding that given milling is a new
> strategy, some players can't understand how to win with that
> consideration.

Well, you'll have to explain that very thing before the rest of your
position makes any sense. I've never seen the kind of thing you're
talking about is any discernable advantage to the miller's prey.

> People can and do come back from being milled out.

And how would they do that, with no library? I've been inviting
you to point that out to me pretty much since this part of this
thread started? I can bloat back from being down to one pool.
Or just get ousts despite the fact I'm down to one pool.

Sometimes, if you're right on the verge of ousting someone, you
might do it with just the permanents you have on the table. But
it's usually unlikely, much more so than making ousts after having
been bled down to one pool.

> Another question: Does Paul sit at tables where From a Sinking Ship is
> used? Collatoral pool damage? Unblockable bleeds for X? Tension in the
> Ranks? Any number of random pool point things? (Intellectual curiosity:
> what kind of deck is this?)

What, you're about to construct some argument around, "What does Paul
do if someone has the exact correct hoser card to stop him?" I don't
know, I've never seen it. I suppose he'd probably lose but who knows?
Maybe he packs lots of Sudden Reverses.

Either way, I don't care. The point pretty much speaks for itself
whether a silver bullet card exists to stop it or not.

> What I want to know from you is: how many times do you see a Methuselah
> come back from 1 pool compared to the number of times that that player is
> ousted? I'd guess no more than about 10% of the time.

Well, a lot more of the time than I see a Methuselah go on to do much
after he's had his whole library waxed in the early game. By far.

>> Bah. No point going on and on with this. Refusal to concede obvious
>> implications of library deprivation is the source of your confusion
>> about why people regard such decks as they do.
>
> Insistence upon postulating that "my word is obviously correct and you're
> a blithering idiot" is unlikely to promote discussion.
>
> I accept implications of library deprivation. I do not accept frothing at
> the mouth, ignorance of positive consequences of a miller, or biased
> interpretations of probability of ousting with limited library.

I'm sorry, but it just doesn't seem like you do. The point I was trying
to make never involved trying to prove milling was unbalanced. If anything,
it's an underpowered strategy, not an overpowered one. But its not the
prey who benefits. It's the rest of the table excepting, possibly, the
grand prey. But usually even the grand prey is better off with a milling
grand predator because your claim that the miller's prey is so "freed"
from the miller's strategy is wrong. Especially because miller's prey
usually does the logical thing and goes straight backwards because he
knows he's not going to be allowed to oust his prey in peace, even if
he's allowed to come close. The miller will use Eagle's Sights, Life
Boons, and other tricks to prevent it. Any indirect actions he takes
geared towards ousting his prey faster (e.g. equipping with laptops),
will be intercepted. This is not "bias" this is reality.

> To me, that seems like an *ideal* scenario to earn not one vp, but
> possibily two, three, or the table. You're of course ultimately reigned in
> by the size of your ever-depleting library, but it's usually not fast
> enough to prevent you from taking your due. A miller is in a classical
> game sense not a predator at all. Not for about 12 turns.
>
> Refute that. You haven't done so yet.

Refute what? Your conjecture that things are just hunky-dory for the
miller's prey. OK, I'll refute it with my own conjecture: things aren't
hunky dory. I don't know where you got "12 turns" as the amount of time
he has nor how you figured out he was totally unfettered in all these
wonderful ways. He's not. He just has different challenges, assuming
his predator's deck is very effective.

> Call it dazzling if you wish, but it won't help you to have a correct
> understanding of table state when a miller is your predator. A miller
> always prefers a prey who feels as if he can do nothing, and so, in fact,
> does nothing.

I don't care what he "feels like". That sounds like a stab at another
unsubstantiated argument, presumably that "the whiners are screwing
themselves by not acting when they could" or something. I'm not saying
it hasn't happened. Perhaps it has. Or perhaps it's just a form of
whining in its own right - that prey tend to go backwards for
completely understandable reasons instead of selflessly going forward to
gather what VPs they can before contently sacrificing themselves when
they prematurely run out of library, like lambs to slaughter. Whatever.

Fred

Messages.Author: Tom Duncan
Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> I think maybe the bone of contention over combat isn't so much that
> irresponsible play is bad. The issue is more whether things that
> are as bad as irresponsible play can happen a lot because a well-
> constructed combat deck that is also well-played simply gets unlucky.
>
> Fred

Unlucky how? I'm not so sure I'm picking up what you're throwing down.
Are you saying a good player with a good combat deck who is intent on
surviving his predator and ousting his prey is more likely to get
'unlucky' and ruin his prey's game, trounce his predator, but be
second-ousted by his grand-predator who eventually sweeps?

'Unlucky' for a combat deck is probably having a Dom predator who's
bleeding for 5 and bouncing bleeds on top of that. Combat decks have
have minimal 'everything else', and are obviously going to have trouble
with a power or speed anything, but bleed in particular. It's the same
way a hyper-bleed or Vote & Bloat has limited space for combat -
whichever one is sitting on the right has the advantage.

Just remember - the player with the combat deck starts the game at a
disadvantage, due to the method by which he/she is attempting to oust.
Give that player some props, and extra points for difficulty and
creativity. If you consistently find yourself frustrated and upset by
the manner in which you did not win a game, perhaps you need to
re-evaluate why you play it.

Messages.Body:
"Tom Duncan" <veknp...@yahoo.com> wrote in message news:1136852594....@g43g2000cwa.googlegroups.com...

>
> Fred Scott wrote:
>> I think maybe the bone of contention over combat isn't so much that
>> irresponsible play is bad. The issue is more whether things that
>> are as bad as irresponsible play can happen a lot because a well-
>> constructed combat deck that is also well-played simply gets unlucky.
>>
>> Fred
>
> Unlucky how? I'm not so sure I'm picking up what you're throwing down.

Unlucky by having bad luck. How does anyone get "unlucky"? The issue
is not how one gets bad luck, but what happens when one has bad luck?
And not just to him. People who have bad luck do worse than if they
had good luck. We know that. But what happens to the other players?

> Are you saying a good player with a good combat deck who is intent on
> surviving his predator and ousting his prey is more likely to get
> 'unlucky' and ruin his prey's game, trounce his predator, but be
> second-ousted by his grand-predator who eventually sweeps?

No. Luck, by definition, happens as much to one player as the next.
(Except when one is finagling with definitions, of course. As
frequently happens when people are trying to make points about what
amounts to good play.) I'm saying that an unlucky bleed deck which
accomplishes most of what it's trying to do but loses anyway hurts
its neighbors less than an unlucky combat deck which accomplishes
most of what it's trying to do but loses anyway. In other words,
the key to understanding why people whine about sitting next to
certain non-overpowered decks is understanding what happens when
those deck accomplish what they're trying to do but don't win.

> Just remember - the player with the combat deck starts the game at a

Perhaps. I'm not concerning myself with which decks are how powerful.

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
>> I'm arguing that your ability to get an oust is *enhanced* by having a
>> predator who doesn't affect your minions or pool for many turns. That
>> enhancement is roped in at about the 12 turn mark, but you still have a
>> chance to gain vps and win. You are not totally screwed.
>
> Ah, sorry. I quoted you and then totally missed your point. (I didn't
> notice it until David restated it. Sorry.)

No problem.

> The compensating "advantage" isn't worth the disadvantage. For one
> thing, there isn't much enhancement. In fact, in some ways, it's even
> worse.

Why? I guess I'd like you to tell me in a fairly step-by-step manner why
the specific positive consequences of a milling predator don't constitute
an advantage. I had mentioned these in my last post.

> The only library deprivation deck that even comes close to working is
> one that concentrates on Slaughterhouses, Harbingers, and uses their
> auspex. Since they don't have to go forward for a long while using this
> strategy, they're just giving up some master phase actions to put out
> Slaughterhouses, and sitting back on both defense (which will readily
> include bleed bounces, a form of offense as well that I'll have to fend
> off) and stopping everything I do with intercept.

This isn't of course true. A milling deck gains little from bouncing
bleeds, largely because it doesn't have much forward pressure itself. Its
forward-pressure is orthogonal to your loss of pool. Besides, a wallish
deck's first priority is to not die. In that sense, it must save the
largest share of its resources to prevent its predator from killing *him*.
And, since Harbingers have limited ability to actually torpor people in
combat (without devoting a lot of deck space to it, which is key), it
tends to be defensive in nature.

A milling predator hardly cares what you do, so long as you're not
thwarting its ability to defend itself and lay Slaughterhouses. What are
they going to block? What's the value in stopping anything? They want you
to play more cards!

> Just doing that alone - without the library deprivation - is actually
> another really form of objectionable neighbor strategy: the intercept
> wall. Add library deprivation, and yes, I'm totally screwed. What
> you're trying to argue is some form of compensating advantage is at best
> totally lame and at worst, more injury heaped on top of injury.

Not particularly, no. Unlike the intercept wall deck, a milling predator
has little to no incentive to prevent you from doing your thing. So long
as it's going forward, it couldn't be bothered.

>> I've won many games with 10 or fewer cards. I've won many games with
>> millers as my predator.
>
> I never claimed you couldn't win a game with a miller as your
> predator. I claimed that millers frequently screwed their prey
> even they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them
> as predators.

Yes, and I claimed that bleeders frequently screwed their prey even if

they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them as predators.

And, I claimed that voters frequently screwed their prey even if

they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them as predators.

And I claimed that combat monsters frequently screwed their prey even if

they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them as predators.

Again. . . what's the difference? Can you say that any of my statements
are untrue? What makes milling special?

> As for winning with 10 or fewer cards, we've all done that - when we had
> a whole library of cards to PUT us in that position. If you mean,
> you've won lots of games after a miller hammered your library severly
> and got it down to 10 cards WAY prematurely, I can't speak to that
> because I didn't see the games you're talking about.

Ok, so we're going to allow some sorts of anecdotal evidence but not all
sorts. Fine. Where do you get the WAY prematurely from? Let's look at that
Harbingers deck that mills you dead and see how it does, shall we? Let's
put together an optimal draw:

Turn 1 Info Highway, 6 transfers pops out Agaitas
Turn 2 Slaughterhouse -2 cards total
Turn 3 Slaughterhouse -6 cards total
Turn 4 Slaughterhouse -12 cards total
Turn 5 Slaughterhouse -20 cards total
Turn 6 Slaughterhouse -30 cards total
Turn 7 Slaughterhouse -42 cards total
Turn 8 Slaughterhouse -56 cards total
Turn 9 Slaughterhouse -72 cards total
Turn 10 Slaughterhouse -90 cards total

That is to say, in 10 turns, without using any other abilities or you
using your deck and a perfect draw from your predator, you're completely
decked. This never happens. To play 9 Slaughterhouses in a row is
extremely unlikely. If we look at a more moderate view, you're gonna
get 12 turns. (You get an extra one just if you assume that your predator
doesn't get a god draw turn 1.)

Now, can we please stop arbitrarily refuting the statement about "12
turns"? I gave you the most extreme case above, and even in that case, you
get 9-10 turns. If you moderate it a bit, it's quite reasonable you'll get
12 full, healthy turns of play.

> There could be lots of reasons - like your predator's deck sucked and/or
> he played it badly and/or he got so unlucky, the milling didn't affect
> you that much. Doesn't change anything.

Invalidating games you haven't seen Fred? The real question is, can I do
that to your examples without proof?

> For the record, I'm fine with having a predator who's game is so bad it
> doesn't affect me hardly at all. (Though my prey will no doubt hate
> that.) But if my predator substantial does what he's trying to do but
> just fails to oust me in the end, THAT will undoubtably cripple me far
> more than a bleed or vote deck doing the same thing - which is my point.

No, no, it won't. No more than ANY other strategy would cripple you.
Because you're HOSED on one pool. Most people are HOSED on one pool. Most
people die on one pool. Everyone has a story where they pulled it out. But
the vast majority of cases. . . you DIE on one pool.

>>> Sorry, nope. Not the same thing. As I pointed out, people can and do
>>> come back from 1 pool left all the time. Paul Johnson built a deck
>>> that REQUIRES he play with with one or two pool at all times.
>>
>> I can't assist you with understanding that given milling is a new
>> strategy, some players can't understand how to win with that
>> consideration.
>
> Well, you'll have to explain that very thing before the rest of your
> position makes any sense. I've never seen the kind of thing you're
> talking about is any discernable advantage to the miller's prey.

To be crystal clear: you're not in happy land with a miller's prey. But
compared to ANY DECK THAT MOVES FORWARD, you are in happy land. I have
explained it over and over again:

Wouldn't you love to have a predator that never did pool/minion damage to
you, and instead took X cards from the bottom of your deck (that you
weren't going to play with anyway)? Everyone I know would. Now, a miller
has to mill Y>X cards before it matters to you. Do you realize how much
time that gives you? Lots of time. Lots of toolup. You get to really make
use of that time.

>> People can and do come back from being milled out.
>
> And how would they do that, with no library? I've been inviting you to
> point that out to me pretty much since this part of this thread started?
> I can bloat back from being down to one pool. Or just get ousts despite
> the fact I'm down to one pool.

The way they come back from being milled out is to PROACTIVELY understand
their situation, take their lumps, and go for it. You then have the
freedom to know that you can move with little to no chance of things going
badly for pool/minions because of your predator's inaction. You may be in
a tough spot once you're actually decked, but if you've done your job
before that (which is something that's not often hindered by the miller),
then you're well-set to succeed at a game win.

It's not all that improbable. You just have to prepare differently. Just
like you "bloat" before you lose pool, here, you use your resources before
you lose them. Simple. Straightforward. And, something I've described in
detail over the last 4-5 posts that you haven't yet responded to.

> Sometimes, if you're right on the verge of ousting someone, you might do
> it with just the permanents you have on the table. But it's usually
> unlikely, much more so than making ousts after having been bled down to
> one pool.

You can often hang out and do well. Tell me. . . what does a milling
predator do when his prey have no deck? He sits there, staring at his
Slaughterhouses and waits for his Brinksmanship. That's *another* thing
you can try to knock down. You get extra turns of life and pressure from
permanents, even though you're decked. In an end game, that may be enough.

>> Another question: Does Paul sit at tables where From a Sinking Ship is
>> used? Collatoral pool damage? Unblockable bleeds for X? Tension in the
>> Ranks? Any number of random pool point things? (Intellectual curiosity:
>> what kind of deck is this?)
>
> What, you're about to construct some argument around, "What does Paul do

> I've never seen it. I suppose he'd probably lose but who knows? Maybe
> he packs lots of Sudden Reverses.
>
> Either way, I don't care. The point pretty much speaks for itself
> whether a silver bullet card exists to stop it or not.

I think it's interesting that you consider a single silver bullet when I
mentioned at least FIVE different methods by which Paul might lose a pool
or the game. Three of those are actually larger categories of pool loss,
and don't refer to specific cards at all. No, I'm not asking about silver
bullets. I'm asking how he deals with pool loss when he's at 1 pool.

Well?

If you want to make him an anecdote, then back up your anecdote.
Otherwise, drop him as part of your argument.

>> What I want to know from you is: how many times do you see a Methuselah
>> come back from 1 pool compared to the number of times that that player
>> is ousted? I'd guess no more than about 10% of the time.
>
> Well, a lot more of the time than I see a Methuselah go on to do much
> after he's had his whole library waxed in the early game. By far.

I thought you didn't see many such games. Are you sure you're giving
milling the same historical perspective as other decks?

>>> Bah. No point going on and on with this. Refusal to concede obvious

>>> about why people regard such decks as they do.
>>
>> Insistence upon postulating that "my word is obviously correct and
>> you're a blithering idiot" is unlikely to promote discussion.
>>
>> I accept implications of library deprivation. I do not accept frothing
>> at the mouth, ignorance of positive consequences of a miller, or biased
>> interpretations of probability of ousting with limited library.
>
> I'm sorry, but it just doesn't seem like you do. The point I was trying
> to make never involved trying to prove milling was unbalanced. If

Note that I have never *ever* postulated that milling was unbalanced. I'm
not doing it now. I'm stating that you may still win with a miller behind
you, and that the likelihood of such an event is just as much as in the
bleed/vote/combat case.

> its not the prey who benefits. It's the rest of the table excepting,
> possibly, the grand prey. But usually even the grand prey is better off
> with a milling grand predator because your claim that the miller's prey
> is so "freed" from the miller's strategy is wrong. Especially because
> miller's prey usually does the logical thing and goes straight backwards
> because he knows he's not going to be allowed to oust his prey in peace,
> even if he's allowed to come close.

The miller's prey should move forward. This is the first mistake of the
prey. When a prey decides he can do nothing, the miller wins. This is
precisely when the miller wins. Whether the prey goes upstream or just
sits around, the prey still loses.

> The miller will use Eagle's Sights, Life Boons, and other tricks to
> prevent it. Any indirect actions he takes geared towards ousting his
> prey faster (e.g. equipping with laptops), will be intercepted. This is
> not "bias" this is reality.

A predator that mills *cannot* do that and defend his pool at the same
time and win! And if a miller is doing such a thing, you should consider
similarly bad examples for bleed/vote/combat! An intercept block deck
cannot block multiple people all day and live. It will deck itself
(thereby ousting itself with Brinksmanship), or lose its minions, or run
out of blocks, or be unable to pass its Brinksmanship. It cannot magically
do all of these things.

>> To me, that seems like an *ideal* scenario to earn not one vp, but
>> possibily two, three, or the table. You're of course ultimately reigned
>> in by the size of your ever-depleting library, but it's usually not
>> fast enough to prevent you from taking your due. A miller is in a
>> classical game sense not a predator at all. Not for about 12 turns.
>>
>> Refute that. You haven't done so yet.
>
> Refute what? Your conjecture that things are just hunky-dory for the
> miller's prey. OK, I'll refute it with my own conjecture: things aren't
> hunky dory. I don't know where you got "12 turns" as the amount of time
> he has nor how you figured out he was totally unfettered in all these
> wonderful ways. He's not. He just has different challenges, assuming
> his predator's deck is very effective.

If his predator's deck is very effective, then you'll be ousted. You have
no argument if that is the case, because despite the means, the fact that
he's ousted you means his deck worked. And, I've already stated that
you're not in happy land when you're a miller's prey. You're not in happy
land as anyone's prey. But, among people to be preyed on by, you get more
freedom and flexibility to move and oust and win.

I notice that you're still unwilling to specifically address those
positive consequences of sitting behind a miller. Any reason?

>> Call it dazzling if you wish, but it won't help you to have a correct
>> understanding of table state when a miller is your predator. A miller
>> always prefers a prey who feels as if he can do nothing, and so, in
>> fact, does nothing.
>
> I don't care what he "feels like". That sounds like a stab at another
> unsubstantiated argument, presumably that "the whiners are screwing
> themselves by not acting when they could" or something.

No, it's not a stab. A prey who feels that he can do nothing feeds into a
miller's strategy. That's a simple fact. Because sitting around squanders
your resources. Not moving towards an oust squanders your resources.
That's a fact of the game state.

> I'm not saying it hasn't happened. Perhaps it has. Or perhaps it's
> just a form of whining in its own right - that prey tend to go backwards
> for completely understandable reasons instead of selflessly going
> forward to gather what VPs they can before contently sacrificing
> themselves when they prematurely run out of library, like lambs to
> slaughter. Whatever.

Or they could actually win. Because a miller can't stop you forever. A
milling deck that devotes enough transient cards towards stopping you
risks being ousted him/herself. A miller that takes permanent steps can be
blocked by you and his/her predator. A miller that stops you from ousting
likely dies himself. A miller that has a prey who can activate one of the
6 ways to stop/slow down his deck suffers a great deal because the game
drags on and on. That's something the miller can't afford.

Just out of curiosity, any reason you delete large portions of my posts
that make the points that you consistently refuse to consider, thereby
making me repeat them over and over?



Messages.Author: Fred Scott
Messages.Body:
"Ankur Gupta" <agu...@cs.duke.edu> wrote in message

news:Pine.GSO.4.62.06...@eenie.cs.duke.edu...

>>> I'm arguing that your ability to get an oust is *enhanced* by having a
>>> predator who doesn't affect your minions or pool for many turns. That
>>> enhancement is roped in at about the 12 turn mark, but you still have a
>>> chance to gain vps and win. You are not totally screwed.

...

>> The compensating "advantage" isn't worth the disadvantage. For one
>> thing, there isn't much enhancement. In fact, in some ways, it's even
>> worse.
>
> Why? I guess I'd like you to tell me in a fairly step-by-step manner why
> the specific positive consequences of a milling predator don't constitute
> an advantage. I had mentioned these in my last post.

It isn't something that can reduced to a single statement other than to
say, "There's no reason it needs to be." In a multiplayer game, the
designers - in a strict sense - need only balance the rewards of pursuing
a strategy vs. the costs and challenges from the standpoint of the player
pursuing it. It's nicer if they were to also pay attention to the balance
of problems and opportunities a given strategy one player might pursue
as it affects both his prey, his predators, and his crosstable allies,
but:

1) There's no strict need for it; and

2) It's probably impossible or at least incredibly difficult, which
is probably why it doesn't happen.

In follow-up to #2 above, I'll point out that for instance, an intercept
wall deck is much harder on one's predator than one's prey overall.
On the other hand, a weeny stealth-bleed deck with little or no defense
is certainly much harder on one's prey than one's predator. And in both
these cases, I'd assert that these things are true even taking into
account that metagame choices can be made against both which will trump
each one (as appropriate). But so what? The metagame, looked at as a
basic Games Theory matrix game, isn't balanced (zero sum) in this sense.
That is to say, even if there's no perfect screw-your-predator or screw-
your-prey choices, the choice you make will affect the expected value of
the predator matrix vs. the prey matrix.

I don't know if any of this is clear. I'm using terminoloy and concepts
that I learned about 30 years and probably using them both poorly. But
if you know anything about Games Theory, hopefully this was at least a
foggy description of what I'm getting at.

So, to make a long story as short as I can, the answer is, although I
can see where depriving a HoS player of many of his master phase actions
(and possibly making him expend resources to pursue getting more MPAs)
to the end of getting Slaughterhouses out probably lessens the pressure
on his prey somewhat, it really doesn't lessen it very much. It doesn't
have to. The nature of the task of running one's prey out of cards is
so difficult that to make to something that's possible to accomplish at
all, the designers made the library deprivation part pretty easy to
accomplish. It really doesn't consume many resources. I'm not sneezing
at all the MPAs used, mind you. But it does still leave all their minion
cards free for other purposes - like intercepting a lot of actions and
still having a good supply of combat cards.

I'm not saying I know how to build a good library deprivation deck.
I've never done it myself. But it sure looks to me like Eagle's Sighting
actions your grand prey can't stop is a very reasonable tactic. They
may not be able to do it a lot, but I don't think they have to in order
to simply screw you over (on the road to hopefully breaking through and
ousting you).

>> The only library deprivation deck that even comes close to working is
>> one that concentrates on Slaughterhouses, Harbingers, and uses their
>> auspex. Since they don't have to go forward for a long while using this
>> strategy, they're just giving up some master phase actions to put out
>> Slaughterhouses, and sitting back on both defense (which will readily
>> include bleed bounces, a form of offense as well that I'll have to fend
>> off) and stopping everything I do with intercept.
>
> This isn't of course true. A milling deck gains little from bouncing
> bleeds, largely because it doesn't have much forward pressure itself. Its
> forward-pressure is orthogonal to your loss of pool. Besides, a wallish
> deck's first priority is to not die. In that sense, it must save the
> largest share of its resources to prevent its predator from killing *him*.
> And, since Harbingers have limited ability to actually torpor people in
> combat (without devoting a lot of deck space to it, which is key), it
> tends to be defensive in nature.

All right, again, I'll grant, I don't know exactly what works best.
But it seems to me that Telepathic Misdirections are by far the most
efficient bleed defense. That's why I'd probably be tempted to use
a fair number of them (especially given that they'll help with interception
in a pinch, too). And there is too something to be gained by bouncing
bleeds: it distracts your prey and slows him down. I agree that you're
not going to actually bleed him out unless you're incredibly lucky and
your predator is an incredibly irresponsible bleeder. But anything that
causes him to not go forward as fast can't hurt. In some cases, bounce
may not help in this way at all but I suspect you'll often get at least
some milage out it. And since it's so easy to use, why not?

> A milling predator hardly cares what you do, so long as you're not
> thwarting its ability to defend itself and lay Slaughterhouses. What are
> they going to block?

Eagles sight particularly damaging bleeds or directed actions. Block JS
Simmons, Tasha Morgon, Laptops, or any other bleed enhancers. Block
Mr. Winthrop, Sport Bikes, Ravens, etc. that he'll use to screw with
his prey. Block damaging votes. Any sort of miscellaneous undirected
actions that may be of value to him towards gaining an oust (Army of
Rats, for instance). There's all sorts of ways your untapped minions
sitting around with a boatload of intercept can slow your prey down.
And this is not what I call "no pressure".

>>> I've won many games with 10 or fewer cards. I've won many games with
>>> millers as my predator.
>>
>> I never claimed you couldn't win a game with a miller as your
>> predator. I claimed that millers frequently screwed their prey
>> even they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them
>> as predators.
>
> Yes, and I claimed that bleeders frequently screwed their prey even if
> they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them as predators.

Right - but I disagree, to finish the rehash. Again, bringing my prey
down to a single pool is not like bringing my prey down to his last 10
library cards way prematurely. I'm not going to argue about how many
turns he's had to pursue an oust. I understand 12 turns is the average
length of a game so it seems to that miller who can only get his prey's
library down to 10 cards after 12 whole turns is probably doing a
crappy job. But I haven't sat down and analyzed it. I'm just assuming
the miller has done a very effective job of destroying his prey's
library but failed - just barely - to get the oust at the end.

There are ways to come back from being down to one pool. There are
no effective ways to reconstruct your library.

> And I claimed that combat monsters frequently screwed their prey even if
> they failed to win, which is the reason people hate them as predators.

...on that last claim, I'll agree.

> Ok, so we're going to allow some sorts of anecdotal evidence but not all
> sorts.

I didn't really say that. I'm just saying that although you're experience
is interesting to the discussion, it doesn't prove anything one way or
another because there's could be all sort of mitigating factors that
caused the situations you reported.

> Fine. Where do you get the WAY prematurely from?

Inductive reasoning (and some deductive reasoning):

1) Players using mill decks are attempting to win.
2) Therefore, they must use mill decks because mill decks allow them
to win some of the time.
3) In order to win by milling, they must be able to mill all their
prey's cards away and either bleed them out when helpless or by
some other means, like Brinksmanship. The point is, it doesn't
work unless some of the time, miller succeeds at decking his prey.
4) Luck varies.
5) Because miller must succeed a significant amount of the time,
miller MUST nearly succeed some of the time but barely fall short.
This step of the argument is key. My justifications are:
Average success quantity approximates either a bell-shaped
curve or, at worse, a flat curve. Most likely at least somewhat
bell-shaped. The thickness of the "bell" must favor failure,
since to favor success would allow the miller to at gat least
one oust over 50% of the time, which would be unbalanced. (And
milling would then be a highly popular strategy.) So JUST
BARELY falling short is more likely than succeeding.

Since the miller must succeed a signficant amount of time,
he must just barely fall short even more often.

6) I assert that "just falling short" *IS* causing your prey
to exhaust his library "way prematurely". At least, that's what it
looks like to me. I don't know what you think it looks like when a
miller just misses ousting his prey. It seems to me it would be
very bad for the prey. A milling deck that gave his prey a more than
fair chance at getting ousts wouldn't be a very successful milling
deck.

(ellide logic about "12 turns")

> Now, can we please stop arbitrarily refuting the statement about "12
> turns"?

My point is, I don't care how long it is. Either it must be very bad
for the miller's prey or it isn't a very good milling deck that's
likely to ever win much. I don't care about the latter case so
much because I think misguided, self-ousting strategies tend to be
their own punishment. But I just don't see how this _can't_ be
very bad for the prey.

>> There could be lots of reasons - like your predator's deck sucked and/or
>> he played it badly and/or he got so unlucky, the milling didn't affect
>> you that much. Doesn't change anything.
>
> Invalidating games you haven't seen Fred? The real question is, can I do
> that to your examples without proof?

It's just that there's no way to respond to them. I'm not saying you're
wrong and I'm certainly not accusing you of lying. You may not have
noticed something I would consider to be a corrupting factor. I'm just
saying the relevance of ancedotal evidence cannot be established for these
purposes so it's no use trying to rely on it to back up your opinion.
Absent game trends we can both readily agree on, you have to stick to
logic.

(removed a bunch of stuff that's more rehash...)

>>> People can and do come back from being milled out.
>>
>> And how would they do that, with no library? I've been inviting you to
>> point that out to me pretty much since this part of this thread started?
>> I can bloat back from being down to one pool. Or just get ousts despite
>> the fact I'm down to one pool.
>
> The way they come back from being milled out is to PROACTIVELY understand
> their situation, take their lumps, and go for it.

I guess I'll just have to say, I've never observed that to work for a lot
of reasons I've already listed. At least, I'll say I understand where we
disagree that's hard to reduce to reason. To me, the vast marjority of
decks are just not going to gain much in terms of ousting the rest of
the table from the knowledge that their predator isn't really after their
pool. If you think they can, then that explains a lot.

>> Sometimes, if you're right on the verge of ousting someone, you might do
>> it with just the permanents you have on the table. But it's usually
>> unlikely, much more so than making ousts after having been bled down to
>> one pool.
>
> You can often hang out and do well.

Usually not, no. Again, if you think people often do "well" after they've
been decked, that also explains a lot.

> Tell me. . . what does a milling
> predator do when his prey have no deck? He sits there, staring at his
> Slaughterhouses and waits for his Brinksmanship.

It shouldn't be a long wait. In fact, I expect him to usually have
drawn it by the time of the decking. If the miller hasn't, he's either
built a bad deck or has gotten pretty unlucky.

And what is one supposed to do when one has no library in the mid-game
and one's prey is still alive WITH library. Almost always nothing.
Defense is weak without a library. Offense is almost always non-existant,
unless one has, for instance, Jost Werner with a Flak Jacket or two.

> That's *another* thing
> you can try to knock down. You get extra turns of life and pressure from
> permanents, even though you're decked. In an end game, that may be enough.

How are you even getting to an end game. If you're in "end game", the

>>> Another question: Does Paul sit at tables where From a Sinking Ship is
>>> used? Collatoral pool damage? Unblockable bleeds for X? Tension in the
>>> Ranks? Any number of random pool point things? (Intellectual curiosity:
>>> what kind of deck is this?)
>>
>> What, you're about to construct some argument around, "What does Paul do
>> if someone has the exact correct hoser card to stop him?" I don't know,
>> I've never seen it. I suppose he'd probably lose but who knows? Maybe
>> he packs lots of Sudden Reverses.
>>
>> Either way, I don't care. The point pretty much speaks for itself
>> whether a silver bullet card exists to stop it or not.
>
> I think it's interesting that you consider a single silver bullet when I
> mentioned at least FIVE different methods by which Paul might lose a pool
> or the game.

Absolutely. The deck is not foolproof. So what? No deck is. The point
that it even exists says enough about how viable a Methuselah with one or
two pool can be. It's not intended as proof positive that being cut down
to one pool is better than 5 or 10 library cards way early. I know that.
It just expresses what I think is the reality of death-by-pool vs. death-
by-early-library-deprivation.

> Three of those are actually larger categories of pool loss,
> and don't refer to specific cards at all. No, I'm not asking about silver
> bullets. I'm asking how he deals with pool loss when he's at 1 pool.

My observation was that he had ready answers to almost any form of pool
loss. It wasn't foolproof but it was damned impressive. And it was what
he had to do to make all of his Parity Shifts useful.

> If you want to make him an anecdote, then back up your anecdote.
> Otherwise, drop him as part of your argument.

It isn't intended for the same purpose as yours.

>>> What I want to know from you is: how many times do you see a Methuselah
>>> come back from 1 pool compared to the number of times that that player
>>> is ousted? I'd guess no more than about 10% of the time.
>>
>> Well, a lot more of the time than I see a Methuselah go on to do much
>> after he's had his whole library waxed in the early game. By far.
>
> I thought you didn't see many such games.

I haven't. "Of those I've seen..." is how I intended people to take the
above statement. I will grant that my experience is pretty scant.
Not non-existant, however.

> Are you sure you're giving
> milling the same historical perspective as other decks?

It's more a matter of reasoning how such things work and seeing my
reasoning vindicated in the games I've observed. Again, I will
grant that there maybe angles I haven't seen. I just haven't heard
you say anything to really feel I've missed something.

>> The miller will use Eagle's Sights, Life Boons, and other tricks to
>> prevent it. Any indirect actions he takes geared towards ousting his
>> prey faster (e.g. equipping with laptops), will be intercepted. This is
>> not "bias" this is reality.
>
> A predator that mills *cannot* do that and defend his pool at the same
> time and win!

I've seen players who were not milling and had to win in other ways (e.g.
combat, using lots of combat cards) do it. I have a hard time imagining
why an HoS deck could not just because his master cards are tied up
in Slaughterhouses (but he need not actually cause combat damage, otoh,
unlike blocky-fighty decks).

> And if a miller is doing such a thing, you should consider
> similarly bad examples for bleed/vote/combat! An intercept block deck
> cannot block multiple people all day and live. It will deck itself
> (thereby ousting itself with Brinksmanship), or lose its minions, or run
> out of blocks, or be unable to pass its Brinksmanship. It cannot magically
> do all of these things.

He doesn't have to do it "all day". He just has to block the key things
his grand-prey cannot. Hopefully his grandprey has _some_ kind of
defense, right?

> I notice that you're still unwilling to specifically address those
> positive consequences of sitting behind a miller. Any reason?

Basically, because I don't think they're very positive. I don't think
you get very much acceleration toward ousting your prey. This is not
something that can be reduced to positive proof because it's a broad
statement that addresses the entire metagame and talks about what
happens when an "average" player is _somewhat_ releived of having to
worry (as much) about his predator exhausting his pool.

Or were you talking about being being a miller's predator? If so,
this would be the first time I'd noticed you raising the issue.
Let's see: a deck that has to prey on another deck which is designed
to sit there and intercept everything and slow everything down. My
question would be, "What positive consequences?"

>>> A miller
>>> always prefers a prey who feels as if he can do nothing, and so, in
>>> fact, does nothing.

...

>> I'm not saying it hasn't happened. Perhaps it has. Or perhaps it's
>> just a form of whining in its own right - that prey tend to go backwards
>> for completely understandable reasons instead of selflessly going
>> forward to gather what VPs they can before contently sacrificing
>> themselves when they prematurely run out of library, like lambs to
>> slaughter. Whatever.
>
> Or they could actually win. Because a miller can't stop you forever.

Sure he can. He runs you out of library cards quicky. Then you are
stopped. Forever. The offense of most decks effectively grinds to a
halt when there is no library cards. I guess I take that as a general
truth. Again, if you don't, that explains much of our differences.

> Just out of curiosity, any reason you delete large portions of my posts
> that make the points that you consistently refuse to consider, thereby
> making me repeat them over and over?

I will delete anything that is essentially the same point made further
up in the post or previously in the thread. In short, I do not believe
them to be points I have "consistently refused to consider" (though
clearly I make mistakes from time to time when I just flat miss something).
I suspect at least some of the time, I _have_ responded to them and you
are refusing to consider the response. This is typical of people who
see an issue in vastly different terms. At least, I'm starting to get
some rough ideas of how we see "reality" different. In that sense, we
seem to be making some headway.

Fred

Messages.Body:
"Drace" <Chrysanth...@gmail.com> wrote in messagenews:1136871149.5...@g49g2000cwa.googlegroups.com...

> I'm not even certain where you get the idea that this last part of your

I don't know what this means. It doesn't matter how good they are.
If they're good enough to win or get ousts at all, they're good enough
to wax a library and fail, which is the point.

> Furthermore, if your mill deck is already an intercept wall
> and SOMEHOW preventing you from ousting your prey via it's library
> destruction (which as far as I usually see is doing just as much as re
> randomizing the deck everytime), why the heck would you even need to go
> backwards if he's already able to block everything you do?

You're conflating two different responses that apply to two different
situations in order to create an apparent contradiction. The point
of the eagles sights was suggested as means of slowing your prey
down on his quest to oust his prey. It would apply to key pool
attacking actions by a miller's prey who was geared to launch them
aginst the miller's grand prey. It would apply to situation where
the miller was confident that a combat encounter would not be
destructive to his own minions.

The "going backwards" reference was suggested as a general,
long-term response by the prey of a miller and such actions
would be assumed to be situations at a time of the prey's
choosing where the prey was confident that some hard could be
inflicted on the miller.

And, in any event, I didn't suggest that going backwards was
necessarily an effective response. It all depends. In some
cases, it may not accomplish much but it may be all the prey
can do to gain some measure of revenge. At the very least,
it may accomplish this: it will ensure that his prey is in
a healthier shape to oust HIS prey and destablize the game
in a way the miller likely will not care for.

> And furthermore, why WOULDN'T the prey go forward to gather VP's?

If he doesn't think he can succeed before he's decked (meaning
he probably won't succeed at all), he may reason that it will
only weaken his prey's ability to operate against his grandprey
and/or the (new) HoS predator (after he is ousted). As I
said, revenge.

Fred

> Ok, so we're going to allow some sorts of anecdotal evidence but not all
> sorts. Fine. Where do you get the WAY prematurely from? Let's look at that
> Harbingers deck that mills you dead and see how it does, shall we? Let's
> put together an optimal draw:
>
> Turn 1 Info Highway, 6 transfers pops out Agaitas
> Turn 2 Slaughterhouse -2 cards total
> Turn 3 Slaughterhouse -6 cards total
> Turn 4 Slaughterhouse -12 cards total
> Turn 5 Slaughterhouse -20 cards total
> Turn 6 Slaughterhouse -30 cards total
> Turn 7 Slaughterhouse -42 cards total
> Turn 8 Slaughterhouse -56 cards total
> Turn 9 Slaughterhouse -72 cards total
> Turn 10 Slaughterhouse -90 cards total
>
> That is to say, in 10 turns, without using any other abilities or you
> using your deck and a perfect draw from your predator, you're completely
> decked. This never happens. To play 9 Slaughterhouses in a row is
> extremely unlikely. If we look at a more moderate view, you're gonna
> get 12 turns. (You get an extra one just if you assume that your predator
> doesn't get a god draw turn 1.)

I couldn't resist stopping and studying this. A few weakness in your
analysis:

1) Why does Agaitas need to come out in the first turn, necessitating
(in turn) the play of Info Highway? Admittedly, she supports the
general theme of the deck, but then you turn around and fail to
account for any library she eats up. And - in any event - who cares
whether she comes out the first turn? Play a Slaughterhouse on the
first turn, gaining 2 additional cards every turn of play and use
four transfers per turn, like everybody else. That would speed up
things significantly.

2) Does your prey actually USE any of his own library?!? Mine always
does. Does our metagame differ that way?

3) I know a lot of people just mindlessly build 90 card decks but unless
it's a card-intensive combat deck (which would be that much more vulnerable
to library deprivation), there's no reason you should. Personally, I
shoot for 75-78 card decks and occasionally less that, depending on what
type of deck I'm building.

4) It's not totally ridiculous to think in terms of adding half a dozen
Parenthenons and the turbo-charge the Slaughterhouse play. Of course,
this will interfere with deck reliability in other ways and degrade
your minion card play (so intercept, waking, and combat defense will
suffer somewhat) but it should usually insure that your prey has
very little time indeed to get any ousts.

Granted, you're not going to draw 10 Slaughterhouses (except perhaps in
the Parthenon scenario, given sufficient Slaughterhouses in the deck).
The bottom line is, it's still not clear to me how many turns a
Slaughterhouse deck might take to eat it's prey's library on average.
It might very easily be less than 12, depending on how you built the
deck.

> Now, can we please stop arbitrarily refuting the statement about "12
> turns"?

Decidedly not.

Fred

I feel compelled to share an anecdote.
I recently tested a Tupdog/Gargoyle build that had 2x Jacob the Glitch.
I had never used Jacob, so I figured I'd give him a whirl, and see how
the table responded (not using any tricks to bloat with him, basically
just a cheap Tupdog enabler). The deck was working well, my Gargoyles
were competent blockers and slaves, and when my opponents made me dump
my hand, I simply redrew more of the same stuff and kept playing my
game. I WAS DOING JUST FINE. Then, I was made to discard my hand and
could not replace it all from my library. All in all, I was made to
discard 35 cards. I promply was ousted with three cards in my hand.

while I was running out of cards, and then swarm bled his way to
victory. Not sure how it relates to the discussion, though yubetcherass
I have removed Jacob from that deck.

them. It requires a different mindset, and those points are intended to
encourage that thought process.

> That is to say, even if there's no perfect screw-your-predator or screw-

I'm not sure what your point is though. Sure, your choice will affect the

> So, to make a long story as short as I can, the answer is, although I

> (and possibly making him expend resources to pursue getting more MPAs)

Again, even supposing you had NO counter to your predator's milling

d) drop out Slaughterhouses e) pack intercept f) defend your pool and g)

If they can block. . . three of your actions in the game, I don't call

The thing is, Fred, you don't have to argue how many turns he's had to

> seen HoS decks that do just that.

I don't think Ankur's trying to say that they can't do it in a "it's
not conceivable" sort of way. He's trying to say that they *shouldn't*
do it, for a variety of reasons; i.e. doing so is bad play on their
part (in general) - and bad play is covered elsewhere in the thread as
being annoying in its own right.

I think it's a good point. In general, they want you to burn as many
cards as possible, making their job easier, and spend their own
resources holding back their predator until you're decked. Now, if
you're playing a stealthy deck, they may try to "help" you cycle that
stealth with an Eagle's Sight or whatever, but otherwise, why would
they care if you can oust your prey if it gets them that much closer to
a VP of their own? Sure, beat up his vampires into torpor, bleed him
for 7 at a time, who cares? As long as I survive until the endgame I
get 2 VPs at least, maybe 3 and the win. They really just want to make
sure you don't get 3 in a row and take the GW from them, and otherwise
they should be more concerned about their own pool than the state of
your prey.

In other words, the HoS milling decks you've seen that "do just that"
are playing quite differently from what Ankur would expect of them.
Which explains a lot of where your differences of opinion are.

John

Messages.Author: jnew...@difsol.com
Messages.Body:
Fred Scott wrote:
> I guess I didn't see him suggest why it should be "bad play". He
> seemed to be saying that if the mill deck expends reaction resources
> trying to stop its prey from doing things that are not direct attacks
> on the mill deck, then it wouldn't have enough to respond to its own
> predator as well. And I just don't agree.

You may be right. Again, though, this is the main source of your
contention.

> As for it being bad play, it seems to me the more stable the HoS
> player can keep the game, the better it is for a mill deck. And
> he might get more VPs on the way to a win. So if this is the line
> of argument, I'd want to know why anyone thought it was "bad" -
> as in "irresponsible" or needless affecting things are of no
> concern to the mill deck. They may not be crucial things exactly.
> But they are of legimate concern to him.

Possibly, so long as that "stability" favors him. Trying to slow down
an incredibly fast deck is obviously in his interest in terms of
getting a Game Win, as is speeding up an incredibly slow deck in front
of him (because he needs that first VP to get anywhere, and his prey
playing cards is one of the best ways for him to get there). It's also
(often) good if his prey is the one that appears strongest and attracts
some attention from the rest of the table.

> It's VP they can't get. And the sooner your prey ousts his prey, the
> more the table is destablized. I realize this last statement is kind
> of broad and often not true (and thus the miller is always free to
> judge otherwise, depending on the specific situation) but I think
> as a general rule of thumb, it's accurate. In general, a mill deck
> wants ousts to happen later and less often (except the ousts he makes,
> of course).

So long as he can actually get his own ousts, yes. But the deck (at
least as I understand it) is built on the premise that it's not really
likely to sweep anyway. So your prey needs to be able to play his
cards, and you need to make sure you have enough resources to hold back
your predator. Thus, the HoS deck should try to *slow* your ousts where
he can reasonably do so without overexposing himself (especially if
this makes you play more cards), but should probably not be overly
concerned with *stopping* it unless you're failry certain that you can
also defend yourself from your own predator - which should take a
pretty high priority, since (eventually) ousting your own prey is
practically guaranteed if you surive long enough.

> > In other words, the HoS milling decks you've seen that "do just that"
> > are playing quite differently from what Ankur would expect of them.
>
> I don't know. The tactic makes a lot of sense to me.

Consider this: You indicate that a) the HoS deck should interfere with
your actions to a somewhat large degree and b) the HoS deck will
somewhat often screw you by interfering too much, leaving you little or
no chance to earn VP, and then die to its predator.

Ankur's contention (as I read it) is that if the resources devoted to
a) were instead used to protect the HoS deck from its predator, b)
would happen less frequently and less harshly, allowing both you and
the HoS a greater chance at VP. Having never really played with or
against it, I've no idea what's right in practice, but this seems
reasonable to me in at least a good portion of cases.

It would be interesting to do some sort of comparison and determine
which style actually wins more with such decks.

John

> I'm saying that an unlucky bleed deck which

> its neighbors less than an unlucky combat deck which accomplishes
> most of what it's trying to do but loses anyway. In other words,
> the key to understanding why people whine about sitting next to
> certain non-overpowered decks is understanding what happens when
> those deck accomplish what they're trying to do but don't win.

OK - starting to get you. When the neighbors of the combat deck defeat
it, they find theyselves with some trashed minions in torpor, and maybe
a couple of toothless or armless vampires with 0 or no blood, and
without sufficient minion ability to defend themselves against the
remaining table dynamic, which is probably 'direct Pool damage'
oriented.

I REALLY REALLY REALLY don't want to start up on the mill thing, but
obviously you believe that when the neighbors of the mill deck finally
defeat it, the prey is left with scant few cards remaining in the
library, making it difficult to defend against the remaining table
dynamic, which is likely 'direct Pool damage' oriented.

Conversely, when the neighbors of a 'direct Pool damage' oriented
deck, like your basic Dom bleed or KRC & Cap vote pusher, finally
defeat it, they still have their minions reasonably intact, and their
library available, to defend against the remaining table dynamic, which
is still likely 'direct Pool damage' oriented. But's that's OK, because
that's what you build your decks to defend against.

The only thing I can gather is that the predominance of 'direct pool
damage' strategies, that do not involve direct threats to seconadry
resources, cause players to predominantly pack defenses for said
strategy (bloat and bounce). When the occasional non-traditional
ousting strategy shows at the table, the traditionals scamper to try to
return the game to it's traditional state. If they succeed, the game
has been altered in the process, and does not resemble a 'normal' game.
This is disconcerting to the traditional player, who wonders why people
would want to ruin a perfectly good game of "Bleed Fastest".

To those players, I say "Too bad". The very reason I play non-bleed
strategies is because most decks only pack bleed defense and piles of
bloat (which requires minions, most often). It's a risky play, I'll
grant, because if your predator is hyper-focussed, your in for "one of
those games". Still, attacking minions directly, at it's core, trumps
ALL strategies, because they all require MINION ACTIONS to advance. By
limiting those actions, you limit the decks overall potential. A player
who does not use deck space for combat defense is simply asking for it,
IMO. For Pete's sake, protect your investment!!

I have the priviledge of playing in a high combat meta, where 20
combat cards would be considered 'light', and Fame is almost always
contested at some point in the course of a game. It makes for a very
interactive experience, and extremely intense end-games. IMO, it makes
for a much better game.

Your library is a resource. Just like your Pool and your crypt. You can
limit it if you want to, but would you look through your 75 card
library, realize you only intended to spend 24 Pool, and then say to
the table at set-up, "You know what, guys, I'm only going to play with

if I can, because you never know when you might need your entire
library. The trick is keeping the ratios of card type on target with
your card flow.

For some decks its a definite advantage to have a library under 90
cards, the larger library you have, even if the ratios are exactly the
same between the 90 and the 60 card library, the more likely you are to
get significant deviation from a perfect spread and get more freakish
results as in not seeing any of your card x for 20 cards. Also when you
consider that there may be many 1 per deck cards that you want to cycle
into as fast as posible, smaller libraries are even more attractive as
you are again likely to see these cards sooner.

When I build a deck I will always consider what library size is needed
for that deck type, ie how many of my key cards do I need to play in
order to be able to get the win - then add a bit for good measure, and
build around that. I mean, Ive never beeen able to make a combat deck
that uses transient cards under 90, as you know damn well you may need
all your library to get a win, but for things like walls, WG's and
embrace type decks, 90 isnt required and is detrimental to the decks
performance.

Yeah, it's an interesting quirk of Jyhad players that almost everyone
seems to build their library to the maximum size and their crypt to the
minimum. It's somewhat counterintuitive. I have to admit to being
among the people that do that, largely because I've gotten really well
accustomed to thinking in terms of the numbers one would want in a 90
card deck. I also tend to play a lot of combat-intensive decks (though
seldom rush combat), and my metagame is very combat heavy with a
serious lean towards longer games. That said, I often wonder if going
up to 90 cards is always the best approach, and typically do it anyhow.
The most notable exception in my case was a 70some card weenie/midcap
anarch PRE deck that plunked down Anarch Revolts (old version) and
bloated like hell with Anarch Salon and Tribute to the Master. Games
with that deck tended to be short, though it's been on ice since the
rewording of AR. I sort of wonder if it might actually do ok with that
new wording anyhow.

Regarding ratios. it's worth noting that different library counts have
different prime factors, so if you're looking for exact ratios certain
numbers are unlikely to work. For example, if I felt my deck was
optimal at 90 cards with 9 copies of Ascendence, and I wanted to cut
the deck to 70, the new optimal count would be 7. However, if I had 3
copies of Ascendence, and wanted to cut down to 70 I would be hard
pressed to decide whether or not to cut a copy, since the ratio would
be skewed at either 2 or 3.

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
CthuluKitty wrote:
> Yeah, it's an interesting quirk of Jyhad players that almost everyone
> seems to build their library to the maximum size and their crypt to the
> minimum. It's somewhat counterintuitive.

There is incentive to build your deck to the maximum size--barring the
vagaries of clumping theory (that is of dubious impact with the large
deck sizes), there is minimal difference between using a 45 card deck,
or two identical 45 card decks shuffled together, except that in the
second instance, you are much less likely to run out of cards. It is
true that you are unlikely to run out of cards in a given game with 90
cards, let alone 70, but that you *can* run out of cards, the incentive
to build a maximum size deck is concrete.

With your crypt, you are unlikely to ever run out of crypt cards at
12--it is rare that a player gets out more than 5 or 6 vampires in a
given game, so there is almost no incentive to make a crypt larger than
the minimum. I've run out of library cards plenty of times in games of
VTES. I have *never* run out of crypt cards. And with the small size of
crypts, the clumping issues become more concrete--with 2 of a vampire
in a 12 card crypt, it is impossible to draw into 4 of them in your
opening crypt; with 4 of a vampire in a 24 card crypt, while it is
unlikely, the possibility of drawing all 4 in your opening crypt is a
possibility, providing concrete disincentive to build an identical
twice as big crypt.

-Peter

This is definitely true. The clumping issue, I think, revolves more
around card types than anything else, though. Specifically master
cards, and to a lesser extent action cards (and to a far lesser extent
any other type of card.) Master cards are often used as single copies,
making it desireable to cut the total number of cards in a deck, and
jamming on masters is the bane of most players, making it undesireable
to run a bunch in your deck. That said, I still run damn near all my
decks at 90, with at least 16 masters (utilizing Life in the City a lot
to avoid jamming) because library cards are a resource. Often if a
game is tight, I'll look to deck someone with combat, and win the
endgame due to increased permanents, usually in the form of masters.

That is one of the other advantages of combat decks, that you can alter
the expenditure rate of library cards by yourself and your opponents.
Of course, this can lead to the longer games and combat heavy
environments that Jesse was refering to, but this is where I argue for
faster play, not fewer turns or shorter time limits.

different (fewer than 12 minions necessary, different transfer rules,

easier proposition. Larger libraries would be fun for combat
strategies, but I think that would just degenerate into abuse of

Messages.Body:
pd...@lightlink.com wrote:
>
> There is incentive to build your deck to the maximum size--barring the
> vagaries of clumping theory (that is of dubious impact with the large
> deck sizes), there is minimal difference between using a 45 card deck,
> or two identical 45 card decks shuffled together, except that in the

> cards, let alone 70, but that you *can* run out of cards, the incentive
