I tend to agree with you, Peter, but I wonder what a statistical
anylsis will show. I'll take a crack, not knowing at the beginning
what the results will be (this, of course, could be dangerous - as any
lawyer will tell you, never ask a question to which you don't already
know the answer).

There are several metrics which might show what the difference is
between different library sizes, but for the sake of argument, I'll
pick one. The chance of drawing a given card in your opening hand is
always something of interest to Jyhad players - especially with cards
like Information Highway, which are unique and highly useful at the
start of a game. This is also an area that is very strongly effected
by deck size.

As luck would have it, an article by "Chance" on the topic is archived
at Mark & Judith's Jyhad page (last updated circa 1998 ;)), though the
formatting isn't conducive to this particular question (the point of
that article was mostly to tell you how many Info Highways to put into
your deck based on its size). I'll list the results by size of deck
and proportion of the card in question (I used 5%, 10%, 20%, except in
cases where 5% wasn't a whole number). The numbers that follow are the
chances of drawing at least one, the chance of drawing exactly one, and
the chance of drawing more than one of the given card.

40 card deck, chance of 1+, chance of 1, chance of 2+
5% (2 cards) -- 32.31%, 29.62%, 2.69%
10% (4 cards) -- 55.22%, 41.79%, 13.43%
20% (8 cards) -- 81.95%, 38.88%, 43.07%

50 card deck, chance of 1+, chance of 1, chance of 2+
6% (3 cards) -- 37.04%, 32.25%, 4.79%
10% (5 cards) -- 54.57%, 40.77%, 13.80%
20% (10 cads) -- 81.33%, 38.43%, 42.90%

60 card deck, chance of 1+, chance of 1, chance of 2+
5% (3 cards) -- 31.54%, 28.19%, 3.35%
10% (6 cards) -- 54.14%, 40.12%, 14.02%
20% (12 cards) -- 80.94%, 38.13%, 42.81%

70 card deck, chance of 1+, chance of 1, chance of 2+
5.71% (4 cards) -- 35.03%, 30.32%, 4.71%
10% (7 cards) -- 53.85%, 39.68%, 14.17%
20% (14 cards) -- 80.65%, 37.92%, 42.73%

80 card deck, chance of 1+, chance of 1, chance of 2+
5% (4 cards) -- 31.18%, 27.53%, 3.65%
10% (8 cards) -- 53.63%, 39.35%, 14.28%
20% (16 cards) -- not calculated

90 card deck, chance of 1+, chance of 1, chance of 2+
5.56% (5 cards) -- 33.94%, 29.27%, 4.67%
10% (9 cards) -- 53.46%, 39.09%, 14.37%
20% (18 cards) -- not calculated

Chance did not calculate probabilities for more than 15 copies of a
card in your deck, and I decided that the tediousness of computing
those probabilites was probably not worth the minor gain, since the
trends had already been established.

A few things to take away from this data:
-The ~5% line only has 3 data points of any real value, although the
values for 50, 70, and 90 data points do well to illustrate the fact
that certain ratios of cards are only possible for certain deck sizes.
The difference between a 40 card and 80 card deck in drawing *at least
one* of the given card is 1.13% (in favor of the 40 card deck). The
difference in probability of drawing *exactly one* is 2.09% (again in
favor of 40 cards). Only a ~1% gain for cutting the deck in half seems
dubious at best.

-The 20% line has an odd effect... with this many cards in your deck,
the *greater* the deck size, the less chance that you will draw more
than one of the given card. This isn't true for 5% or 10%. Basically
it just means that your 40 card deck with 8 Torn Signposts is more
likely to draw 2 of them first turn than your 90 card deck with 18 Torn
Signposts. But your 90 card deck with 9 Deflections is more likely to
draw 2 of those than the 40 card deck with only 4 Deflections. Not
sure exactly what the effect of this on deck building might be. In
either case, though, the difference is minimal.

-The 10% line is the most interesting, because it has the most data
points, and represents the most common quantities of key cards in most
decks. Going for the extremes, the difference in the chance to draw
*at least one* of your Deflections first turn, between a 90 card and 40
card deck is 1.76%, while the difference in the chance to draw *exactly
one* is 2.70%. That's not a lot of difference. To normalize this a
little bit, 2.7% is about a 7% increase on the original percentage,
while 1.76% is about a 3% improvement. Assuming you're particularly
interested in drawing *exactly* one, we'll say that a 40 card deck is a
7% improvement on a 90 card deck in this regard.

Note that those are absolute extremes. 40 card decks aren't even
tournament legal, and if you're not doing crazy stuff with Pochtli,
Waste Managment, Reinforcements, and/or Summon Soul, it's not enough
for nearly any deck. A 60 card deck is only about a 2.6% improvement
on 90 cards, and 80 cards is only about a 0.7% improvement.

The question is whether or not this improvement is worth it. If you're
100% unlikely to ever run out of cards, then even a 0.7% improvement is
worthwhile. However, if 1% of decks are mill decks, or include some
milling component, those 10 cards will be worthwhile to you at least 1%
of the time. Personally, most of my decks will run down to the last 10
cards almost everytime I am not ousted before I get that far. So if
I'm an average player who is the last-man-standing approximately 20% of
the time, I will need every card I can get almost 20% of the time (not
including times where I am milled, or go through my deck exceptionally
fast and then get ousted).

But this depends on your deck, of course. Combat decks will tend to
churn though cards faster than most. Bottom line, this analysis
suggests that if your metagame contains *any* mill decks at all, play
with 90 cards everytime. If you haven't seen a mill deck, decide if
you're going to get enough benefit (generally from 1 to 7%) out of a
smaller deck size to outweigh the chance (deck dependent) of you
running through your entire deck.

Of course, there are other metrics for measuring the benefit of a
smaller deck, but most of them are going to be considerably more
complicated. One way might be to calculate the aggregate possibility
throughout the game of each card drawn being a particular card, or the
possibility of that card being distinct in your hand, or being
sufficiently varied from what you've drawn so far - all of those would
be mind-numbing to calculate, but they could be done. People can talk
about the "flow" of a deck, but until you have some sort of statistical
or empirical evidence to back it, I don't see that it means much.

> about the "flow" of a deck, but until you have some sort of statistical
> or empirical evidence to back it, I don't see that it means much.

Yeah, it's clearly very complicated on the math end, and I appreciate
the preliminary data analysis you posted. The biggest problem with it
is that it only concerns what you're likely to draw in your first 7
cards. Math like that does well for figuring out appropriate crypt
ratios since most of the time you'll be relying primarily--if not
entirely--on your first 4 vampires. It seems much less appropriate for
the library since you'll be drawing and playing cards from it
throughout the entire game.

The best reason that I can think of for running fewer than 90 cards
concerns unique cards more than clumping. Various decks will perform
much better when they manage to get certain unique cards reasonably
early in the game, but it's very dangerous to run more than 1 or
perhaps 2 copies of any such card.

In any case, there are certainly good arguments for always building to
90. What I don't like is that so many people, myself included, do this
without thinking about it. Ideally, players would think through the
logic of each and every step in deck building, and deciding an
appropriate number for the library is one of the things that should be
considered, instead of just taken for granted.

(Ventrue HQ?), you could run 1 in a 45 card deck to maximize your

you'll need three backups), but then you are really only going to have
that many of a given unique if you *really* need to have it, and then I
suppose if you need it, drawing the extras can be dealt with via
discards.

Well, it only specifically addresses the first 7 cards, but it is
equally applicable to any 7 cards in the library (when taken
independently from the rest of the library), so it does address the
possibility of clumping. Also, it's my hypothesis that this metric is
highly dependent on library size, and so it should be an indicator of
the data that would be found by more complicated metrics.

Your point about unique cards is definitely valid. If you have a 60
card deck with 2 Hunting Grounds in it (assuming you really need your
HG), it may not be worth it to put 3 HG's in your 90 card deck, because
2 of them are dead draws. On the other hand, I've played a deck with 4
Alamut's in it - sometimes you just have to be resigned to discarding.
Again, it depends on the likelihood of your deck running out of cards
(and sometimes on whether or not you own enough of the cards in
question), but I normally choose not to worry about having 2 or 3 dead
draws in a deck - that card could just as well be an extra stealth card
I don't need, or a 3rd PA when I only have 2 vamps, etc... And then,
in some cases, there are a few different unique cards that do the same
thing. You can add J.S. Simmons, Tasha Morgan, and Robert Carter (and
non-unique Laptops). You can add WMRH, KRCG, and Rumor Mill. You can
add PB: Montreal, PB: Baranquilla, and PB: Mexico City (if you're into
that sort of thing). A 40 card deck might not have room for 3 (or 5?)
intercept locations. A 90 card deck may have a similar ratio of
intercept locations, so it has almost the same chance of getting 1 out,
but it can also get 2 or 3 of them out by the end of the game, which a
40 card deck may not be able to.

Another wild-card is cards that allow you to shrink your deck at will.
Barrens, Fragment, Dreams, Aura Reading, Lear Jet, Katherine Stoddard,
several other vampires that let you discard... Including some of these
cards in your deck will decrease the small drawbacks of having a larger
deck, since you can selectively shrink it during the game.

I said that this was an analysis of your "opening hand", which was
perhaps a mistake. It's actually the analysis of any given 7 cards in
your deck, whether they're the first 7 or the last 7 or somewhere in
between. The chance of having 2+ of a given card in any 7 card slice
is a good indication of the chance of clumping. To find out how long
you will have to wait before drawing card X, ~90% of the time, we would
figure out 2 standard deviations away from the average time to draw
card X (starting from any point in the deck). That's actually not the
hardest calculation in the world, and maybe I'll do it tonight if I get
a chance, though it's been a while since college statistics class -
I'll have to look up the formulas. But I will go on record right now
as saying I'm sure it's not very much improved for a 40 card deck vs.

> > or empirical evidence to back it, I don't see that it means much.
>
> Why? If you're winning and losing games based on card flow, it's
> absolutely critical.
>

*IF*, yes. More likely you're perceiving that you're winning and
losing games based on the perception of card flow. Card flow has a lot
more to do with stuff like per-card opportunity cost, having the
correct proportions of card-types, most of your minions being able to
play most of your cards, using cards with multiple applications, etc...
Sure, if you include that, then card flow is a huge part of winning
and losing. If you tell me that it "feels like" a 60 card deck flows
better than a 90 card deck... that doesn't really mean much. Poker
players may tell you that it seems like AK in the hole *always* loses
to a small pocket pair, but statistically, it's a coin-flip - they just
happen to remember the times that they lose a lot more strongly.

I don't have time to get into any stats analysis right now either, but I
think your earlier work may be leaving out another important factor in
card-play: the percentages you calculated for "any seven cards in the
library" don't take into account the fact that in VTES, cards are replaced
when played and the windows for playing different cards affect the
playability of other cards that may also be in your hand. That is, the
makeup of the seven cards that happen to be in your hand at any one time
affects which of those seven cards are currently playable, which in turn
affects which cards are going to become playable when you draw replacements
in the course of the game.

as complete nonsense. :-) What I'm trying to say is, it's important in
VTES not only whether you have 1 or 2 or 0 copies of a particular card in
your hand when you draw 7 random cards. It's also important what
combinations those cards create, and how frequently you'll re-assemble
combinations as you go through the library, given card-flow rates that
result from your particular set of of minions, permanents, and hand.

Josh

I think I understood. From what I've read, I think some people haven't
been considering it. Considering including X copies of a unique card is
something to think about, but also all copies of all unique cards in
the deck. Expanding on the Alamut example, if I include 4 Alamuts in a
90 card deck to help draw it early, I know I might run into 3 cards I
have to discard later in the game. Now if I also include 4 Market
Squares and 4 Assamite Hunting Grounds (not saying you'd do this, just
follow with me), once I get Alamut, Market Square, and HG in play, I
have 9 cards in my deck that are essentially dead cards. If an average
game is 12 turns, I'll have to use most of my discard phase actions
just to clear cards that I can't play. A 60 card deck with 3/3/3, will
only have up to 6 cards to discard once it gets one of each in play.
Without cards like The Barrens in your deck, you have a limited
resource in Discard Phase Actions which you must compare against
something you can control, like deck size and the risk of decking
yourself.

Now going from uniques to card types, we can see how clumping can
really screw you. If it is your turn, reaction cards in hand are all
but worthless (if I see I have Wakes in my hand, I might tap more
minions, so knowledge gives some value, even if I can't play it now).
So during your turn you play cards that are not reaction cards and have
y% chance to replace it with a reaction card. I am creating a virtual
minus hand size for myself, which in turn makes it harder to play the
other cards in my hand.

I wish I knew the math to see how 60 cards vs 90 cards works out, but
if 33% of your deck is one card type you have 20 cards vs 30 of one
type. With 30 cards you are more likely to clog your hand out with
cards of a specific type during any given turn. And if you clog your
hand too badly and then can't play those cards, it takes a long time to
clear the jam. Combat decks face this all the time with number of
rushes vs number of combat cards.

Since I can't prove anything, I'll stop here. Maybe some with the math

> blue-moon games where it would make a difference.

> can't bear to remove cards from it, even though it's a good idea
> on balance.
>

In a toolbox deck, particularly one that uses the barrens, aura
reading, infernal pursuit, or something similar, it is useful to use 90
cards just to fit in all your tools. It isn't so much that you plan to
use every card, rather that you plan to use your discard phase to dump
the things you don't need. I've run decks with moderate intercept
before, with 3-5 permanent intercept cards and 10-12 transient
intercept, and used discard phases and aura reading to dump the excess
if I wasn't facing heavy stealth.

I know the tendency around here is for optimized decks, but for a more
generalist deck that plans to use discards, 90 is a fine size.

-Dave Clooney

One tournament deck I built was designed to run out of cards when I score
my last VP, and in the meantime provide that much better card flow. It
turned out to be around 67 cards in the end, had the punch, and was
generally better in more games than a 90-card version would have been.
Sure, I did lose every now and then because of a stalemate situation
depleted my library and the 20-some extra cards my opponents had proved
to be decisive, but in the majority of cases I scored what I could
before actually running out of cards (or won with less than a full hand,
as it happened sometimes).

I guess one point could be, if you bolt some flush tech and a tangential
angle on top of an otherwise compact deck, you'll end up with more
flexibility at a cost to card flow. If you don't include flush tech,
your card flow may suffer even more.

>> on balance.

(meant to say, it's NOT a good idea, on balance)

>
> In a toolbox deck, particularly one that uses the barrens, aura
> reading, infernal pursuit, or something similar, it is useful to use 90
> cards just to fit in all your tools. It isn't so much that you plan to
> use every card, rather that you plan to use your discard phase to dump
> the things you don't need.

Hmm. That's an interesting idea but I don't think it's exactly right
unless you're building kinds of decks you'd expect to run out of cards
even with 90 cards. (In which case, it may not be so good to use things
like The Barrens.) The problem with the concept is however many extra
cards we're talking about will still wind up at the bottom of your deck,
not helping you and just making things more random and therefore bad.

For instance, say you're considering adding 12 more cards to a 78-card
deck for the sole purpose of varying your toolbox cards more widely.
There's only three possibilities in any given game you will play with
this deck:

1) You will not run out of cards at all, whether it has 78 or 90 cards.

Where this is the case, all you're done is add 12 extra cards that
wound up at the bottom of your deck or randomly caused one of your
original 78 cards to wind up there in its place. This is totally
bad except insofar as one of the new cards turns out to be the one
you happened to need that game in place of one of the original 78.
The chances of this happening and helping you are, at best, a wash
with the chances that a new card is drawn and not wanted in place
of one of the original ones that was needed (unless your original
78 cards were poorer choices than the additional 12, which shouldn't
be the case).

2) You would run out of the original 78 cards just using The Barrens
and the like but the additional 12 cards prevent this.

I can see where this would be an improvement. The way I think about
this myself is to say that I'm adding The Barrens for my card churn,
which is what's good about The Barrens. OK, now how many cards do I
need in the deck to make sure I usually don't run out? More than 78?
Then I better have more than 78 cards in the deck. If the number is
90 or higher, then I better have a 90-card deck.

3) You would run out either way, but faster with the 78-card deck.

If The Barrens (and other such cards) makes even 90-card decks run
out a signficant amount of the time, you may want to reconsider if
you want to use them. But you'd certainly want the 90 card deck,
sure.

In practice, I've usually found that card churners don't make my
78-card decks run out very often. Therefore, if I want the card
churners, I add them but don't bother increasing the deck size.
(I suppose that means I might want to consider reducing the size of
my decks that don't have card churners like that but I guess I don't
think about the issue that finely.) As always, it depends on what
you're doing, though. I can see where they might cause problems
in certain types of decks if you didn't increase deck size.

By the way, another card that I've found is just as good or a better
card churner than The Barrens is Dreams of the Sphinx. In the types
of decks I build and the types of games I seem to get into, the six
sure immediate card draws in three turns tend to be enough better
than the one-per-turn over time to justify the pool spent on it.
Depending on how many churners I'm prepared to add, I usually choose
Dreams as my first one, Barrens as my second, and then more copies
of Dreams beyond that. (I don't usually use decks that would make
use of Aura Reading so I don't know where that fits.)

Fred
